clinical_context: Female patient diagnosed with cirrhosis of the liver, uninsured, and not expected to survive beyond the end of the year without a liver transplant. Patient does not drink or use drugs. Seeking information on organizations, charities, medical groups, or insurance companies that can assist with liver transplant for an uninsured patient in immediate need.

28-year-old female, ex-smoker, non-drinker, 5'3", 200lbs, reports intermittent arm pain occurring immediately after sneezing, affecting either or both arms with a somewhat intense ache, and seeks reassurance regarding concern.

3.5-year-old white male, average height and weight, no medications or known medical issues. A bump on his neck, likely at a lymph node location, has been present since at least early August. The bump has remained unchanged or slightly increased in size over several months, is unilateral (not present on the other side), and non-tender to touch. There was no recent illness prior to noticing the bump, and it is uncertain if the bump was present before August. The pediatrician advised watching the bump after receiving a photo and description via email. The parent is seeking guidance on whether to pursue further evaluation, such as bloodwork, or if monitoring is sufficient.

24-year-old female with health anxiety and panic attacks, experiencing perceived abnormal heartbeats during episodes. Blood pressure is normally within range, although occasionally elevated when nervous. Extensive cardiac evaluations over the past year include: stress test, multiple EKGs (some during symptomatic periods), 2-week Holter monitors, echocardiogram, and blood work, all yielding normal results. Asks if it is reasonable to conclude that her heart is likely healthy, given the absence of abnormalities despite thorough testing. Additionally, mentions needing to lose weight, but notes that current symptoms were also present when she was a thinner high school athlete.

55-year-old female, overweight, with normal blood pressure and cholesterol levels, not currently taking any medications. Experiences daily heart flutters, approximately once a day, with normal cardiology test results. Seeks guidance on when to consider anticoagulant therapy, such as Plavix or Eliquis, to prevent stroke risk due to potential atrial fibrillation (A-fib).

39-year-old male, 260 lbs, Eastern-European ancestry. Reports persistent tinnitus in left ear for approximately 2 years, which began suddenly without preceding noise exposure or hearing loss. Also experiences occasional clicking in the same ear when swallowing. Tinnitus is modulated by jaw movement. Has tried nasal steroid sprays for suspected Eustachian tube dysfunction with no improvement. Additionally, has explored TMJ as a potential cause with a dentist, using a night guard, but without relief. Recently used an ear cleaning kit with a camera to visualize the eardrums, noting two hairs appearing to touch the left eardrum, which corresponds with the affected ear. Seeks advice on whether these hairs could be causing the tinnitus and if there is a straightforward method for removal.

25-year-old male, 5'7", 171lbs, overweight. Natural sleep-wake cycle: bedtime between midnight-1am, 1-hour sleep latency, wake-up time 10am, resulting in usual feeling of being well-rested. Recently started a stressful job 6 weeks ago, requiring a 6:45am wake-up time. Has attempted to adjust sleep schedule to 11pm bedtime on weekdays, but experiences persistent fatigue, waking up feeling unrefreshed and mentally impaired. Seeks advice on how to adjust his internal clock to wake up at 6:45am and improve sleep quality.

8-year-old white female, 78lbs, no current medication. Presents with ongoing symptoms following hospital discharge. Initial presentation included 5 weeks of fever, rash, and arthralgias. Symptoms progressed with increasing fever (max 103.5°F), muscle pain (particularly in right leg and arm), and swelling in right knee and index finger. Rash was described as blotchy, pink, and transient, spreading from legs to trunk, arms, and face. Laboratory tests revealed elevated DNase B antibody (547) and ASO titer (300), but did not meet clinical criteria for rheumatic fever. Other lab results included negative strep culture, negative ANA and rheumatoid factor, elevated CRP (8.6 mg/dL) and ESR (80), elevated ferritin (663), and normal CBC, hepatic panel, and LDH. Infectious workup (Parvo, CMV, EBV) was negative. Clinical examination showed a salmon-colored transient rash and a 2/6 ejection murmur, deemed a flow murmur by cardiology. Patient was diagnosed with suspected systemic Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA). Oncology consultation did not indicate further evaluation due to normal cell lines and lack of hepatosplenomegaly. Patient is currently experiencing ongoing pain and inability to walk, prompting concern for worsening condition.

33-year-old Caucasian female, 176cm, 80kg, with Type 1 diabetes (using insulin pump since age 1), polyneuropathy, retinopathy, and Hashimoto's disease. Medicated with duloxetine 60mg, novorapid insulin, ramipril 2.5mg, bisoprolol 5mg, alpha-lipoic acid 600mg, and B-complex vitamins. Diagnosed with diabetic neuropathy at age 15, initially experiencing manageable symptoms of tingling, burning sensations, and reduced temperature sensitivity in extremities. Two years ago, localized pain developed in the upper arm, below the shoulder and above the elbow, initially brief and infrequent. Pain has progressed, spreading throughout the arm and shoulder, causing inability to lift the arm, insomnia, and significant impairment in daily activities. Pain is exacerbated by movement, particularly lifting, but subsides when the arm is still or held against the body, allowing for some functional use. Seeks clarification on whether this severe, activity-dependent pain is related to her underlying neuropathy.

16-year-old male reports experiencing speech difficulties since undergoing surgeries at ages 14 and 16, attributing the change to anesthesia. Symptoms include difficulty thinking of words, processing words, and speaking them, indicating a potential minor aphasia.

25-year-old female, with a history of childhood abuse and neglect, resulting in lack of dental care education. Presents with poor dental health, including a decaying front right tooth and a missing second-to-front left tooth (due to a fallen baby tooth at age 21). Has significant dental anxiety and self-consciousness about her teeth. Seeks guidance on accessing dental care despite financial struggles. Has limited experience with dental visits, having only visited a dentist once as an adult for sepsis due to an infected wisdom tooth. Requests information on the dental consultation process, pricing, and options for affordable care in Australia.

30-year-old female, 5'8", no medical issues. Sustained a head injury approximately 1 hour prior to posting by running into a metal bar at the playground, striking the top of her head with significant force, as reported by her husband from 30 feet away. Did not lose consciousness. Currently experiencing a large bump on the head, headache (described as not severe), and feeling "off", which may be attributed to anxiety. Additionally, reports soreness at the base of her neck. Seeks advice on whether to seek medical attention or monitor her condition, considering the location and force of the impact.

31-year-old female fell backwards on the subway on 10/13, injuring her hand on the railing. Initially experienced significant pain, which resolved by the next day. Now presents with intense, unusual bruising and a painful lump (7.5/10) at the site of injury. The lump is tender to touch, but otherwise, there is no pain; full range of motion is preserved, allowing wrist flipping and fist clenching. Seeks advice on whether an X-ray is necessary.

26-year-old male, weighing 80kg, reports a new underarm bump noticed today, associated with discomfort when arms are closed, tenderness to touch, and mild pain. Experienced fleeting feverishness this morning and fatigue, which may be attributed to work or life stressors. Recently sexually active within the past week, using protection for intercourse but not for oral sex. Denies previous similar underarm bumps, but notes regular sweating and working out. Seeks evaluation for potential causes, including STDs such as HIV, and guidance on necessity for immediate STD testing due to concern for a potentially serious condition.

21-year-old female experienced her first unprovoked tonic-clonic seizure on September 17. The episode began with a severe headache above her right eye and on the back of her head on the left side, which did not improve with 600mg ibuprofen. While putting in an earring, she became dizzy with tunnel vision, lost consciousness, and exhibited stiffness, groaning, and upper body convulsions. Her boyfriend reported her face turned blue, prompting him to start CPR; however, she regained consciousness after the third compression. Post-seizure, she experienced intense anxiety, exhaustion, and a worsened headache. Despite reporting these symptoms to a telehealth doctor, who confirmed it as a tonic-clonic seizure, a nurse practitioner at her physician's office attributed the event to fainting. 

Less than three weeks later, on October 6, she experienced her first migraine, characterized by pain above her right eye, sound and light sensitivity, dizziness, lightheadedness, muffled hearing, ear pressure, and vision changes, which persisted into the next day. She is seeking professional insight due to concerns about the relationship between the seizure and migraine, particularly as her family and the nurse practitioner have been dismissive of her experiences.

35-year-old male, 5'7", approximately 280 pounds, white. Diagnosed with cellulitis on foot at urgent care yesterday, started clindamycin 300mg three times a day. Now notices red swelling on lower leg as well, within 24 hours of initiating antibiotics. Also taking bupropion 300mg daily. Non-smoker, non-drinker, no recreational drug use. Concerned about rapid spread of symptoms despite antibiotic treatment, considering visiting the ER.

21-year-old Indian male, 5'8", 68kg. Sustained a minor bite from a stray puppy's teeth on the lower shin 3 days ago, with no visible scratches or pain reported. The puppy is approximately 1-1.5 months old, born to a stray dog on the college campus where the incident occurred. Seeks advice on whether to undergo rabies treatment.

27-year-old female, 5'10", 140lbs, with immunoglobulin A deficiency (stable with normal levels since twenties). Presents with recent urinary frequency and mild bladder cramping. Urine tests showed large leukocytes, leading to prescription of Bactrim, currently on day 4/5 of treatment. Despite improvement in symptoms (reduced leukocytes to trace amounts, no flank pain), developed a low-grade fever (99.9°F) last night, which decreased to 99.1°F with Motrin and remains between 99.1-99.5°F today. COVID-19 test was negative. Asks if low-grade fever during UTI treatment is concerning.

30-year-old male reports being physically assaulted, resulting in facial injuries, and possibly experiencing a loss of consciousness or altered mental status ("lost some time"). He is currently confused and having difficulty articulating his concerns, seeking general guidance.

39-year-old white male, smoker, 5'7", 200 pounds (recently dropped to 196). Presents with chronic gastrointestinal symptoms, including diarrhea, floating stool, cloudy water after bowel movements, excessive flatulence, watery diarrhea, stomach gurgling, and bloating. Has experienced significant weight loss (4 pounds) and increased urination over the past week, although attributes increased urination to increased water intake. Noted presence of an unknown substance (possibly oil or mucus) floating on water after bowel movements. 

Has undergone extensive testing, including: 
- CBC (3 times)
- CMP (1 time)
- BMP (2 times)
- Urine test (1 time)
- A1C
- Thyroid function tests (2 times)
- Lipase and amylase levels
- Magnesium level
- Celiac blood test
- CT scan with IV contrast and barium
- Colonoscopy
- Right-sided abdominal ultrasound
- Abdominal X-ray

All tests were conducted last year. Patient is concerned about the possibility of pancreatic cancer or another type of gastrointestinal cancer, and seeks reassurance regarding his symptoms, particularly the weight loss and diarrhea.

25-year-old male involved in electric skateboard crash, colliding with a pole. Presents with suspected hernia, minimal pain, and ecchymosis (purple discoloration) at the site of injury. Has attempted to push the hernia back in, but hesitant to apply further pressure due to unusual sensation. Considering delaying medical evaluation until the next day, but seeking advice on whether emergency room visit is warranted.

25-year-old male from Germany, 174cm, 70kg, with no known health issues except a recent strong cold (2-3 weeks ago) treated with Paracetamol and Ibuprofen. Presents with intermittent, itchy blisters on right hand, accompanied by tingling sensation and no pain. Additionally, reports itchy spots on other parts of the body over the last two weeks, mostly without visible bite marks or blisters. Concerned about the blisters on his hand potentially worsening. Seeks possible causes for these symptoms.

Late 30s male, practicing martial arts, with no underlying health issues and taking no medications. Developed toe pain 3 days ago, followed by pus drainage 2 days ago. Initially treated with Epsom salt soaks and cleaning, resulting in temporary improvement. However, upon puncture, significant additional pus was released. Currently, the toe remains swollen, but appears improved after applying antibiotic cream. Concerned about potential severity, seeking advice on whether to seek immediate medical attention or wait an additional day.

18-year-old male, residing in Italy, unvaccinated against Covid-19 and unsure about childhood vaccinations, despite mother's claim of receiving mandatory vaccines as a child. Exposed to anti-vaccine views from family members, but personally open to vaccination. Has experienced depressive episodes, particularly during lockdowns, which have affected his motivation and ability to prioritize health. Has had multiple negative Covid-19 tests, despite close family members contracting the virus, including a grandfather who died from Covid-19 complications amidst pre-existing poor health. Seeks convincing information on the importance of Covid-19 vaccination and guidance on obtaining the vaccine, as well as potential catch-up vaccinations. Requests understanding and non-judgmental advice due to his unique circumstances and mental health struggles.

7-year-old female patient presenting with stomach pain, cough, cold, and intermittent fever (temp responsive to Calpol). Has a history of asthma. Initially attributed stomach pain to muscle strain after a school trip last Thursday. Recently evaluated at an emergency walk-in clinic, where examination, urine sample, and COVID-19 test were unremarkable. Doctors noted tachycardia and elevated temperature, suggesting a probable viral infection, and prescribed erythromycin. Despite treatment, patient continues to complain of stomach pain, which is not associated with bowel movements. The pain location is described in detail, but not explicitly stated here. Patient's family is concerned and seeking advice on whether to seek further evaluation at A&E.

21-year-old male, 103kg, white, Croatian, smoker, coffee drinker, currently taking headache medications. Reports change in bowel habits from normal 2-3 stools per day while working to 6+ stools per day with variability between hard and watery consistency when not working. Seeks explanation for this change.

27-year-old African American male, recently quit drinking and smoking, diagnosed with high blood pressure. Presents with extreme fatigue, tiredness, left atrial enlargement, and daily heart palpitations. Laboratory results show: elevated protein (8.3), elevated red blood cell count (6.51), normal hemoglobin (15.1), normal hematocrit (47.6), low MCV (73.1), low MCH (23.2), low MCHC (31.7), elevated RDW (15.8), normal platelet count (270), and normal MPV (10.4). White blood cell count is within normal range (4.7). Expresses concern and anxiety about laboratory results.

21-year-old Asian female, 48kg, 156cm. Reports history of recurrent UTIs over the past year, initially attributed to Mycoplasma hominis infection diagnosed in her boyfriend. Both partners completed prescribed medications. After a brief period of recovery, patient experienced another UTI, which was treated with antibiotics. However, she developed another UTI 2 weeks later. Seeking alternative management options to avoid repeated antibiotic use.

26-year-old male, 6'3", 280 pounds, reports sudden onset of symptoms over the past day. Experiences sweating, tachycardia (constant heart rate of 120 bpm, even at rest), lightheadedness, and dizziness with mild physical exertion, relieved by lying down or sitting. Additionally, complains of frequent urination (every hour) despite minimal water intake. Concerned that symptoms may be related to a heart attack, given his weight and unhealthy lifestyle, but also considers the possibility of a prolonged panic attack.

25-year-old female reports waking up with numbness in fingers, primarily affecting the left hand, specifically the ring and pinky fingers, for at least a couple of weeks. The numbness occurs upon waking, either in the morning or once during the night, and resolves with shaking. Bilateral hand involvement is noted, but symptoms are more pronounced on the left. Additionally, she experiences tingling sensations in the center of her arm during the day when her elbow is bent, which persists despite attempts to shake it out. Her sleeping position is typically on her right side with her right arm bent and her left arm alongside her body or with her elbow bent. She has a history of heart palpitations, generalized anxiety disorder, and anemia. She is seeking advice on whether this could be carpal tunnel syndrome and is looking to avoid unnecessary hospital visits and expenses due to health anxiety.

17-year-old male living with roommate diagnosed with mononucleosis (mono). Concerned about transmission risk and seeking guidance on precautions. Questions whether they can share a shower, even at different times, due to potential spread through water droplets. Considers wearing masks in and out of the room for both himself and roommate. Wants to know duration of necessary precautions, which would need to last at least until their housing contract ends in 2.5 months. Also considers moving to a new room to avoid infection. Has history of frequently getting sick when roommate engages in late-night activities and parties. Seeks advice on managing the situation and preventing transmission.

34-year-old white female, 5'5", 110lb, taking Lexapro 20mg daily and Adderall 10mg as needed, no alcohol or drug use. Presents with tachycardia, palpitations, history of trauma, ADHD, and family history of heart disease. Symptoms suggest dysautonomia, possibly triggered by prior trauma and stress, with primary complaints of palpitations and occasional dizziness/lightheadedness. Planned diagnostic tests include echocardiogram and Holter monitor, followed by initiation of Toprol 25mg daily (with option to increase to 50mg after 2 weeks) and reassessment of symptoms in 6 weeks. The physician notes a moderate risk of morbidity associated with prescription drug management.

17-year-old male accidentally ingested a single 2cm long, cooked, dull, and soft toothpick while eating lunch. The toothpick was used to hold sausages together and was forgotten in the food. Now, in the evening, he is seeking reassurance due to a friend's alarming comment, despite knowing it's unlikely to be fatal, and is experiencing paranoia about potential consequences.

25-year-old female reports unexplained weight loss over a few months, now stabilized, accompanied by constipation and hematochezia (blood in stool). Her doctor has ordered an abdominal and pelvic ultrasound to investigate these symptoms. The patient is seeking information on potential diagnoses or findings that the ultrasound may reveal.

17-year-old male, 5'4", 160lb, white, residing in the southeast U.S., occasional recreational drug user (via smoking). Presents with a lingering cough that began 3-4 weeks ago, after an illness onset around September 30th, characterized by initial symptoms of sneezing. The cough is described as soft and quiet, yet causing noticeable body convulsions. It has been persistent for a couple of weeks, worsening over the past hour, and is accompanied by throat discomfort. The patient reports coughing every few seconds, with water providing no relief. Prior to this illness, the patient had a minimal history of coughing. Friends have also observed the cough, confirming it's not just the patient's perception. The patient is concerned about potential lung damage due to ignoring early warning signs.

28-year-old female, 5'10", 200lbs. Presents with a perianal mass, initially described as a small bump ("butt nugget"), which has increased in size over time. Episodes of bleeding are associated with further enlargement, suggesting a possible external hemorrhoid. Currently experiencing pain and discomfort, particularly after bowel movements, leading to avoidance of eating and defecation. Patient is uninsured and seeking guidance on where to seek medical attention, considering a walk-in clinic. Expressed embarrassment and anxiety about discussing and presenting her condition to a healthcare provider.

20-year-old white British female, 166cm, 65kg, taking Citalopram 10mg and Lansoprazole 15mg PRN. Experiences recurrent cold-like symptoms every 3 weeks or sooner, including runny nose, sharp nasal pain, constant clear mucus in throat, tiredness, and recent onset of slight cough due to frequent throat clearing. Uses hand sanitizer and washes hands regularly. Finds temporary relief with Neti pot and tablets containing phenlephrine and guaifenesin. Symptoms significantly impact work and quality of life. Seeks opinion on whether symptoms could be related to nasal polyps.

26-year-old Middle Eastern female, 5'3", 114 pounds, with Hashimoto's disease controlled on 50mg levothyroxine. Non-smoker, occasional drinker, no recreational drug use. Never received HPV vaccine due to cultural assumptions and previous practice of protective sex. Inquires about the possibility and worth of receiving the HPV vaccine at her current age, considering her autoimmune condition.

26-year-old male, 5'5", 159lbs, with pre-existing heavy heart and anxiety issues, currently recovering from surgery. Concerned about potential health risks from inhaling marijuana smoke from a driver, specifically whether it could exacerbate existing conditions. Seeks information on how to discuss this issue with his doctor.

30-year-old male reports a 1-week duration of sore throat, runny nose, green mucus, and elevated temperature, with slow improvement. Provides a visual of his throat for assessment, seeking determination if symptoms are consistent with a viral upper respiratory infection or if antibiotic treatment may be necessary.
28-year-old male taking Amoxicillin Clavulanic acid. Plans to consume alcohol while on medication and wonders whether to skip a dose or continue taking the medication as prescribed while drinking.

21-year-old female with congenital brachial plexus injury, status post surgical repair as an infant. Residual deficits include limited finger movement, inability to lift wrist or raise arm above head. Recently developed severe burning sensation in arm, accompanied by muscle twitching and pulsing in arm, fingers, and chest, over the past couple of months. Additionally, notices movement of breast and vibration of posterior muscle when moving index finger. Seeks evaluation of these new symptoms, questioning potential positive implications.

26-year-old female, 177cm, 55kg, White. Reports a hard, round, immobile bump behind her right ear, first noticed 5 years ago. The bump is non-tender to touch, but painful with pressure or prolonged wearing of glasses. Has observed potential increase in size over the past year, which she attributes to either actual growth or perceived change due to weight loss. Expresses concern about possible malignancy. Provides photographic documentation of the bump.

26-year-old male, 5'8", 145 pounds, with a history of crippling anxiety and depression, recently considering potential bipolar tendencies. Currently taking lamictal 75mg, lithium 300mg, and gabapentin 900mg for mental health. Experiencing medication-induced constipation since increasing lamictal to 75mg. Seeks advice on management, specifically wondering if Colace would be helpful.

23-year-old male, normal BMI, no underlying conditions. Experiencing significant anxiety while dealing with an upper respiratory infection (URI). Has had multiple illnesses in the past 4 months, including COVID, a minor viral infection, bronchitis, and the current URI. These illnesses were contracted despite being previously healthy, with only one illness in the preceding 2-year period during lockdowns. Recent increase in stress and poor diet noted. Partner has not contracted any of these illnesses. Patient is concerned about potential leukemia or cancer due to frequent illnesses, but denies bruising, bleeding, or shortness of breath. Seeks advice on whether to consult a primary care physician (PCP) for evaluation.

24-year-old male, 5'10", 165 pounds, mixed martial artist with an upcoming fight in November. Sustained a laceration to his left index finger requiring 3 stitches at his day job. Seeks advice on protecting the stitches during vigorous grip-related training and heavy sweating. Has access to liquid bandage, finger-shaped gauze, and various types of tape, including kinesio tape. Previously discussed concerns with doctor, but language barrier limited understanding of recommended activity modifications, making it difficult to adhere to potential advice to reduce activity.

22-year-old Caucasian female, 5'6", 207lbs. Reports a one-time event of transient vision loss, occurring during an episode of excessive dizziness and weakness while walking. Vision in both eyes intermittently disappeared, never simultaneously, with complete loss of vision in the left eye for approximately 30 seconds. Subsequent blurred vision persisted for about 2 hours, followed by a headache behind the left eye, described as pulsing and varying in intensity. Patient has a history of active bulimia (3-4 purge days per week) and uses vape and smokes weed. Works in electrical and considers potential dust exposure as a possible contributing factor. Seeks reassurance regarding the possibility of this being a benign incident, due to financial constraints delaying medical evaluation until weeks-end.

19-year-old Caucasian female, 5'4", 115lbs. Presents with fever of 40.3°C, severe vomiting, headache, and altered mental status. Medical history includes severe car crash 2 years ago resulting in pneumothorax (2 broken ribs puncturing lung) and spinal cord injury, requiring 3 months of wheelchair use. Occasionally uses Dilaudid as needed. Recently tested negative for COVID-19. Notably, patient has a history of poor immune function and has never had a fever above 39.5°C previously. Initially suspected to have stomach flu, but ultimately diagnosed with meningitis, which caused respiratory distress in the ambulance. Currently hospitalized and intermittently awake, with doctors expressing hope for recovery due to prompt intervention.

23-year-old male reports experiencing symptoms for 3-4 months, including decreased frequency of bowel movements and foul, unusual odor of stool and flatulence, described as a "sickening weird death smell". No rectal bleeding or severe abdominal pain noted. Additionally, complains of persistent fatigue despite adequate sleep, caffeine intake, and outdoor activity with vitamin B12 supplementation. Denies recent changes in diet aside from consuming cheap junk food with poor nutritional balance. Expresses concern about potential colon cancer due to online research, but is deterred from seeking medical evaluation due to financial constraints, including inability to afford a doctor's visit, colonoscopy, or potential chemotherapy. Seeks advice and guidance.

35-year-old male, previously healthy with no underlying medical conditions, no drug use. Suffered a concussion 3.5 weeks prior to death after falling off bed and hitting head on bedside table/wall. Had a history of previous head injury resulting in brain bleeding. Despite recommendations, did not seek medical attention for concussion. Exhibited post-concussion symptoms suggestive of potential brain bleeding, which can be delayed and life-threatening. Two weeks after concussion, became unresponsive and barely breathing, prompting paramedic intervention and life support. Died in ambulance en route to hospital. Cause of death pending coroner's report, but suspected to be related to complications from concussion and potential brain bleeding.

27-year-old black male, 6'0". Presents with a small lesion on his lip, persistent for one month, non-irritating. Patient has a history of frequent marijuana use. Concerned about the lesion's persistence, seeking differential diagnoses aside from herpes or cold sore.

18-year-old female taking bupropion and iron pills, started three weeks ago. Experiences daily episodes of chest pain, rapid heartbeat, strong beats, palpitations, and abnormal rhythm while at rest. Has pre-existing supraventricular extrasystole, which has worsened in frequency and severity since starting bupropion. Psychiatric provider is unaware of the pre-existing condition. Concerned about potential interaction between bupropion and supraventricular extrasystole, seeks advice on whether to schedule an earlier appointment with psychiatrist, currently scheduled for the fourth week of treatment.

35-year-old male diagnosed with an ear infection and prescribed 1000mg of amoxicillin twice daily for 10 days. Shortly after starting antibiotics, pain increased, and a ruptured eardrum occurred, accompanied by a "water draining" sensation, sound, and initial clear fluid discharge, which progressed to pus and minimal blood over a few hours. Approximately 16 hours post-rupture, heavy pus leakage persists. Patient seeks guidance on expected duration of purulent discharge, citing online estimates of 1-3 days, and inquiring about typical expectations for the amount and duration of leakage during the healing process of a ruptured eardrum due to an ear infection.

28-year-old male, 5'11", 78kg. Reports spraining ankle due to a fall with twisting mechanism, experiencing delayed onset of pain starting the next day. Can walk without issue, but experiences pain when moving ankle sideways. Notably, no swelling or bruising is present. Doctor recommended 2-3 weeks of rest and potential use of a foot brace. Seeking guidance on optimal recovery steps.

24-year-old male, 6'3", approximately 200lbs, white, physically active. Experiences uncontrollable vomiting after consuming alcohol, particularly with harder liquors or stronger beers. Can tolerate light beers like Modelo or Budweiser, but reacts to stronger beverages, even after minimal consumption (e.g., one IPA or a couple of beers). Symptoms include excessive vomiting, sometimes requiring ER visits due to inability to retain fluids. Seeks clarification on whether this is related to alcohol intolerance or potential liver issues.

50-year-old female with history of prescription medication abuse and alcoholism, past cancer (fully recovered), and multiple sclerosis (MS). Admitted to hospital in August due to jaundice, diagnosed with liver failure, which progressed to multiple organ failure by Sunday, requiring induced coma, mechanical ventilation, blood pressure medications, and dialysis for renal support. Seeks information on likelihood of mortality and survival rates for multiple organ failure.

38-year-old male planning to undergo a 21-day water fast. Recently obtained a DEXA scan to establish a baseline for body composition. Interested in conducting before-and-after blood tests to track changes beyond weight loss. Seeks guidance on what blood tests to request to obtain useful and interesting results related to the effects of the water fast.

Individual, traveling for four months, witnessed a suicide aftermath on a train at approximately 10 AM. Despite initial expectation of emotional distress, they report feeling confused, detached, and emotionally numb since the incident, with difficulty processing their emotions. Normally an empathetic person, they express concern about their lack of emotional response, describing it as feeling like their brain is "covering up the memory." They recall the event vividly but describe it as feeling "vague" and disconnected. The individual is unsure if their reaction is indicative of traumatic shock or if they are overreacting. Currently, they are experiencing emotional numbing, with no feelings of sadness, anger, or annoyance, which is unusual for them. Seeking clarification on whether their symptoms could be related to traumatic shock.

19-year-old white female, iron deficient with a level of 6 (normal range 20-200), reports never bruising easily, despite multiple blood draws in arms and hands over the past 2 weeks, with small veins requiring several attempts. Has a history of iron deficiency for several years. Recalls bruising only twice in her life, including a childhood incident of breaking her arm. Expresses concern about her inability to bruise, given her anemia diagnosis, which would typically increase bruising tendency. Seeks explanation for this phenomenon, particularly after undergoing prolonged needle procedures (4+ hours) without developing bruises.

26-year-old female presents with a 17mm lymph node in the neck, located near the jaw, which has been present for approximately 2.5 years with significant growth over the last 1.5 years. The lymph node is described as rock-hard yet moveable, and non-painful. Additional smaller, pea-sized lymph nodes are noted around the neck and trapezius muscle. Patient reports persistent exhaustion, but no other symptoms. An ultrasound was performed, with the report describing the lymph node as "normal appearing" despite its size. Patient is concerned about the implications of the 17mm lymph node size and seeks reassurance pending follow-up with her doctor.

Individual used a neti pot with tap water almost daily for three months (November to January) and developed a nasal rash that resolved within a few days. Subsequent diagnostic tests, including MRI, CT scan, and extensive blood work, revealed no abnormalities. Patient is concerned about potential infection with Balamuthia mandrillaris due to similarities with a reported case. Despite resolution of the rash, patient continues to experience anxiety and persistent worries about their health, reporting not feeling well. Seeks advice on whether to continue worrying or reassurance.

26-year-old male, weighing 115lb, reports taking 1000mg of acetaminophen (2 x 500mg pills) once daily for the past week and a couple of days for a recurring headache. He plans to consult his doctor the next day. Concerned about potential medication overuse headaches or liver damage due to consecutive daily use, despite not exceeding half the maximum daily dose. Worries that his lower weight may affect the safe dosage. Seeks information on the safety of taking 1000mg of acetaminophen for more than 10 days. The headache is possibly attributed to excessive screen time (phone, video games, laptop) and stress related to a recent breakup, poor mental health, unemployment, and health anxiety. Requests guidance on whether it is safe to take another 1000mg dose without risking harm.

37-year-old female presents with a newly discovered lesion on her left lateral thigh, characterized as raised with irregular margins and asymmetry. The lesion is located in an area where she has never had a mole or freckle before. Patient has a history of multiple sunburns in her teens and early twenties. She has scheduled an appointment with a dermatologist, who performed an excision of the lesion and estimated 5-7 days for results, considering possibilities of malignancy or a benign cherry angioma.

24-year-old male, 6 feet tall, 85-90 kg, European descent. Presents with persistent pain at the bottom of the tailbone (top of intergluteal cleft) for 6 days. The pain started suddenly after using a potentially unclean toilet. Patient message:

A 51-year-old white man presents to the clinic with a 2-year history of a painful, recurrent rash on his fingers. He initially noticed redness, irritation, and pustules around his nails that he thought were caused by an infection. However, the rash progressed to affect the nail bed, eventually destroying his nails. On examination, well-demarcated, scaly plaques with associated pustules and nail atrophy are present on the right second and third distal digits. He is otherwise healthy.

An 8-year-old male child is brought to the clinic for the third time in 4 months presenting with red-brown papules with an overlying mica-like scale on the ventral side of his arms and legs. His medical and family histories are otherwise unremarkable. His mother states that when the macules and papules go away, the skin where the lesions were previously located is typically lighter than before.

A 24-year-old white female graduate student presents with erythematous, papulopustular patches of skin in a muzzle-like distribution surrounding the mouth, chin, and glabellar region. The lesions are tender to palpation, associated with a stinging and burning sensation, and are aggravated by exfoliating facial washes. Two-year treatment history includes a variety of topical antibiotics, azelaic acid cream, retinoid agents, benzoyl peroxide preparations, topical corticosteroids, and oral tetracycline for cyclic recurrences of outbreaks. These treatment methods were previously successful with complete resolution of each outbreak; however, at present the lesions are persisting despite treatment.

A 20-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a circular hypopigmented lesion on her right cheek. The patient stated that she used to have a mole in the same location. Over time she noticed a white area around the mole that enlarged to the current size of the lesion. After a few months she noticed the mole in the center of the lesion had disappeared. On further questioning, she denies any personal or family history of skin cancer.

A 29-year-old woman with a history of acne presents to the clinic with 3 discrete, atrophic, blue-tinged plaques on her face. The plaques were located on her forehead and cheeks bilaterally. The patient states the lesions had been present for several months and had slowly worsened until they stabilized at their current appearance. The patient reported that the lesions occurred after she went to a physician for “acne treatment.” The patient has no other medical conditions or relevant social history.

A 22-year-old woman complains of an itchy rash on her leg for 4 weeks. She is a collegiate swimmer and had a prior ringworm infection during her freshman year. She has been using over-the-counter antifungal cream for the past 3 weeks with no relief. Multiple round, erythematous, scaling lesions are present on her right leg, some of which are vesicular and weeping. Potassium hydroxide (KOH) test is negative for a dermatophytic infection.

A 62-year-old African American man presents to establish care and to undergo skin examination, which he reports receiving regularly since his sister was diagnosed with melanoma. Examination reveals 3-mm hyperpigmented horizontal bands across the nailbeds of all fingernails, which he reports have been present since his 20s. He denies experiencing any other nail changes or pain. He takes no medications, and he has no history of skin cancer or suspicious moles. He has no relevant medical history.

A 60-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 1-cm long horn-like projection coming from the skin on the superior aspect of the skull just lateral to midline. The structure is yellowish-white in color and feels very firm to the touch. He states that he noticed a small, hard lesion a few months ago and that it has grown progressively larger from the time of initial presentation to now. The patient denies any pain at rest but states that he experiences pain when the lesion is struck accidentally.

A 20-year-old male with a medical history of diabetes mellitus type 1 presents with ecchymosis and bullous lesions on his back, posterior legs, and buttocks. He was playing football when he ran into another player and became unconscious. He was immobile in the hospital for 3 days before he regained consciousness. He has about 7 tense blisters with areas of surrounding erythema on the back, buttocks, and posterior thighs.

A 6-year-old Caucasian boy is brought to the clinic by his parents for dry, scaly skin that has persisted for the past 2 years despite the use of commercial moisturizers. His scaly skin is especially notable over his lower extremities, back, and elbows. The patient denies any pain over the affected areas and reports only a mild itch that is soothed with cold water or lotions. The parents report that he had a similar condition as an infant throughout his entire body and that he has siblings who also have persistently dry skin. His parents have tried exfoliating the scales with moderate success, but the scales recur shortly thereafter.

A 7-year-old healthy boy is brought to the dermatology clinic by his parents after having had a 3-week history of a rash. The patient’s rash was slightly pruritic, and it involved predominantly the trunk, starting as one larger pink patch with fine scale and subsequently spreading with smaller similar macules and patches. The boy’s palms and soles were spared of the rash.

A 15-month-old boy presents with a history of skin blistering since birth, primarily on his hands, feet, and the perioral face. Blisters and erosions also involve the trunk, some in an annular configuration. There is no family history of neonatal blistering or skin fragility. Over time, the patient has had a decreased number of new vesicles and bullae associated with trauma and friction but has developed thicker skin on the soles of the feet and dystrophic nails.

A 71-year-old Caucasian man with myelodysplastic syndrome and on chemotherapy with azacitidine presented to the hospital with 2 days of high fever and 4 days of worsening skin lesions. The lesions appeared on the elbows as “blood blisters,” which grew larger and more painful. He denied any other new medications. He was placed on broad spectrum antibiotics by infectious disease physicians out of concern for ecthyma gangrenosum, and dermatology was consulted. On examination, violaceous, edematous plaques with a central pseudovesicle were seen on the bilateral elbows. Punch biopsies were performed for tissue culture and histology.

A 37-year-old man without a significant past medical history presents to the dermatology clinic with an itchy rash on his right hand that he has had for about 4 months. He had tried numerous over-the-counter hand creams and hydrocortisone cream with no improvement. Additional questioning revealed a 1-year-history of dry, itchy feet. As a construction worker, he wears occlusive, steel-toed work boots and often wears gloves. He is also right-handed. Examination of his hands reveals a normal left hand and a scaly right palm. Diffuse, fine, dry white scale was present on the plantar aspect of both feet.

The patient is a 46-year-old woman who presents at your primary care office for an examination with a single lesion that appears on her left arm. During the examination, it is revealed that the patient has a large sclerotic, indurated, hyperpigmented, anhidrotic, and hairless plaque on the right dorsal forearm. The patient states that these lesions had previously been slightly pink for several months before they had turned brown in color and had become “hard.” The patient has type 2 diabetes, but she has no other medical problems. In addition, she has no relevant social or family history.

The patient is a 21-year-old male who presents for continued acne therapy. He has had severe acne on his face, chest, and back for years. He is happy with his current acne regimen of topical tretinoin, topical clindamycin, and oral minocycline. He has been on the regimen for years. On examination, you notice significant blue-black discoloration confined to sites of previous acne scars. The patient has no other medical problems and no relevant social or family history.

A 53-year-old woman presents with a rash on her left lower extremity that has been present for several weeks. The patient is a native of Brazil and immigrated to the United States in the past month. She states that the rash is painless and does not itch. On examination, the patient has multiple, raised, hyperpigmented papules on the left lower extremity. There is a large, atrophic, hypopigmented patch on her lower shin, at the site of a previous large ulcer. The superior lesion is the newest, and is beginning to ulcerate. She has no other medical problems.

A 6-month-old infant presents with 2 weeks duration of erythematous papules on the soles of both feet and in the toe web spaces. On examination, a single burrow is visible on the left sole. Multiple family members also complain of a pruritic rash that has been bothering them for several months. The family members have tried multiple over-the-counter creams and remedies without success. The patient has no other medical problems or relevant family history.

A 42-year-old man presents with a four-day history of experiencing headache, malaise, and stabbing right-sided headache. Two days after his initial symptoms appeared, he developed a rash over the area of pain. He reports that he went hiking through the Texas hill country prior to becoming ill. The patient is otherwise in good health and has an unremarkable medical history. Physical examination reveals unilateral erythematous, thin, raised plaques over the right forehead. In addition, he has no relevant social or family history.

The patient is a 12-year-old Hispanic girl who presents with a 6-month history of nail dystrophy involving all of her fingernails. On examination, all 10 of her fingernails exhibit longitudinal ridging, pitting, fragility, thinning, and distal notching. The patient’s mother is very concerned about the cosmesis of her daughter’s nails. The patient has no systemic symptoms. On review of systems, the patient’s mother noted that her daughter has started to develop circular patches of hair loss that appear to resolve on their own. The patient has no relevant social or family history and does not take any medications.

A 1-year-old boy presents with a single, L-shaped, yellow-orange hairless patch over the left preauricular skin. The patient’s mother notes that he has never grown hair in that location. The mother is concerned because the area used to be smooth, but seems to be changing. The patient has a history of prematurity and low birthweight but is otherwise healthy. The patient has no relevant social or family history.

An 8-year-old African-American boy presents with a 3-day history of fever, pain, and a rash on his trunk. On examination, the patient has several fragile, bullous lesions on his trunk, many of which have eroded, exposing erythematous, annular lesions. The patient is febrile and shaking in the office, and he appears to be in pain. He has no other relevant social or family history and does not take any medications. His mother is very concerned about her son.

A 13-year-old boy presents to the dermatology clinic concerned about the development of red, itchy, and sometimes painful bumps on his fingers. He first noted seeing the lesions 2 months prior, in early December. Although the initial lesions have since resolved, new lesions appeared after a skiing trip the previous weekend. The patient is otherwise healthy, with no significant past medical history, and he does not take any medications. Physical examination reveals erythematous, tender papules on the lateral and dorsal aspects of the distal fingers.

A 52-year-old Hispanic woman presents with a 3-year history of a very pruritic rash over her shins bilaterally. On examination, both shins are covered in hyperpigmented papules that have coalesced to form thin, rippled plaques. The patient is very concerned about the appearance of her legs and the intense pruritus in the areas of the rash. The patient has no other medical problems and has no systemic symptoms. She has no relevant social or family history and does not take any medications.

The patient is a 13-year-old adolescent girl who presents with a 1-month history of a dark lesion on her finger. She states that the lesion does not bother her, but she came to the clinician because her mother was very concerned about the enlarging area of hyperpigmentation. The patient has no past medical history, no relevant family or social history, and is otherwise in good health. On examination, the rash appears to be a 1 x 1 cm circular patch of hyperpigmentation with overlying scale on the middle finger. During the past month, the rash has grown in size but remains asymptomatic.

A 72-year-old man presents to the clinic with an intensely itchy rash on his abdomen and chest that appeared 2 months prior. He denies starting any new medications prior to the onset of the eruption and any systemic symptoms. Although he traveled and stayed in hotels recently, he reports that his wife does not exhibit any similar symptoms. Physical examination reveals numerous discrete papules, crusted papules, and papulovesicles on the chest, abdomen, and mid-back. His upper and lower extremities, face, and groin are unaffected.

The patient is a 38-year-old Hispanic woman who presents with a 1-year history of a very pruritic rash over her interscapular area. On examination, she has a circular area of slightly hyperpigmented macules in the interscapular region. The patient complains of pruritus but no pain in the area of the rash. The patient has no other medical problems and has no systemic symptoms. She has no relevant social or family history and does not take any medications.

The patient is a 19-year-old woman who presents with several years of a worsening rash. The rash appears as erythematous, hyperkeratotic thin plaques in a seborrheic distribution. The patient states that the rash is very irritating and sometimes pruritic. The patient’s main complaint is that the rash exudes a malodor. The patient states that her father has a similar rash that he chooses not to treat.

A 35-year-old woman is referred for evaluation and management of a rash involving both axillae. She reports recurring episodes of the same rash beginning in her early 20s. Lesions develop and involute spontaneously. Areas affected included the axillae, neck, and groin. Historically, outbreaks are more common and worse during the summer, and after vigorous exercise. Both her father and brother have the same problem; her brother saw a specialist, but forgot what he was told. Otherwise, she is healthy and taking no medications. Examination reveals moist, red, crusted, and malodorous plaques with fissures in both axillae.

A 44-year-old woman presents for her annual full skin examination. She has a specific concern regarding a lesion on her left lower leg. She recalls having a mosquito bite in that area a few years earlier, but it never went away. The lesion is bothersome only when she shaves her legs and nicks it; otherwise, there is no associated pain or tenderness. Physical examination reveals a firm, flat, pink and brown nodule located on the left anterior proximal shin. The lesion dimples inward when pressure is applied.

A 56-year-old man presents with diffuse pruritic papules involving the upper body, with nose and forehead thickening. Over the past 2 years, he has been evaluated by multiple specialists for dysphagia, reflux, chronic kidney disease, hypertension, and dyspnea on exertion. Examination results are significant for generalized firm, fleshy, dome-shaped papules of several millimeters in diameter, on his forehead, ears, neck, trunk, back, proximal upper extremities, and dorsal hands, with forehead, glabella, and nose induration. Relevant laboratory findings include monoclonal gammopathy on serum immunofixation, consisting of immunoglobulin (Ig) G_ and IgA_, and unremarkable thyroid panel findings

A 34-year-old man presents with an itchy rash, primarily on his arms, but also, to a lesser extent, on his face. He denies any fever or malaise, and his medical history is unremarkable. He does not take any medications and notes that he spent the previous weekend doing yardwork on his property, and the rash appeared 4 days later. Physical examination reveals several linear arrangements of papulovesicles on the dorsal and ventral aspects of his forearms with surrounding erythema.

A 62-year-old white man with a past medical history of latent tuberculosis, vitiligo, and psoriasis presents for follow-up for treatment of psoriasis. The patient’s psoriasis has proven refractory to numerous treatments over the years, so he began treatment with secukinumab, a monoclonal antibody against interleukin-17A. After 2 months of therapy, the patient reports new-onset tongue pain. Physical examination demonstrates an erythematous, edematous, diamond-shaped plaque on the posterior dorsum of the patient’s tongue.

A 13-month-old toddler with spreading eczema on his trunk and arms is brought in by his mother. She is applying moisturizer and a cortisone cream. However, 2 days earlier, a wound appeared on his left hand that appears to be infected. Since then, more areas of raw, oozing skin have developed. Examination reveals lichenified scaling plaques scattered on the trunk and posterior knees and arms, and his left arm has monomorphic crusted vesicles and ulcerations on an erythematous base.

A 30-year-old healthy Hispanic woman presents with a slowly progressive facial deformity present since early childhood. She denies any new lesions during this time, any history of trauma to the area, and any family history of similar skin lesions. Examination reveals a bulging, deformed dermal mass with a “bag-of-worms” appearance involving the upper right quadrant of her face, with hypertrophy of the overlying skin and soft tissues. Neurofibromas and café-au-lait macules are not observed.

A healthy 45-year-old woman presents with a several-month history of a small papule at the corner of her right eye. The lesion is asymptomatic and is not enlarging, but she has cosmetic concerns. She denies diplopia, vision loss, or any other lesions on her face and body. Examination reveals a dome-shaped, smooth, translucent papule filled with watery fluid located below the lateral canthus of her right eye.

A 32-year-old white woman who has never smoked presents with pruritic, tender, erythematous, violaceous patches with eczema-like blisters on her upper, lateral thighs. In 2012, she began traveling annually from Pennsylvania to South Carolina, from January through April, where she works with and rides horses daily from morning to evening. Her symptoms began in her first year in South Carolina and appear consistently from January through March. Her lesions appear initially in mid-January as a red dot and progress by mid-February. They resolve spontaneously in March.

A healthy 30-year-old man presents with a 3-year history of an asymptomatic, fleshy papule at the base of his great toe. He denies any new lesions during this time, a history of trauma to the area, or a family history of similar skin lesions. He was treated previously by another dermatologist with cryotherapy; however, he returns to the clinic with recurrence of the lesion. Examination reveals a pedunculated, flesh-colored, well-demarcated tumor on the plantar surface of the base of his great toe.

A 45-year-old woman with insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus presents with a sore on her right leg. She describes a long-standing history of asymptomatic lesions on her shins but had only recently injured her leg, causing the sore, which is slow to heal. Despite a 15-year history of diabetes, she has no systemic complications. She has large, well-circumscribed plaques on her anterior shins bilaterally, which are yellow-brown with telangiectasias and minimally violaceous borders.

A 60-year-old man presents with rapidly growing lesions on his face, trunk, axillae, flexural areas, and groin. The lesions appeared 3 months earlier in his perianal area and extended rapidly to other areas. Previously, he was treated with topical agents for atopic dermatitis and seborrheic dermatitis without improvement. Examination reveals disseminated violaceous papules and plaques on the face, trunk, axillae, and perianal area; some lesions were confluent and ulcerated. Yellowish-red to skin-colored papules are present on the scalp. He has no palpable lymphadenopathy or organomegaly.

A 13-year-old girl presents with a cystic lesion that has been on her forearm for several years. Concerned about the lesion, she reports that it may have grown slightly larger in the past year and it is intermittently painful. More recently, a second similar lesion has appeared in close proximity. She denies any other suspicious lesions elsewhere on her skin. Her family history is negative for skin cancer, and she reports no other medical conditions. Physical examination reveals two well-defined 6-mm nodules that are rubbery, slightly tender, and pink on the right proximal ventral forearm. The overlying skin is intact, and there is no associated adenopathy.

A 62-year-old man with well-controlled rosacea, a monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, and chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL; stable on no current therapy) was seen in the clinic for a full-body skin check. Results of his examination were unremarkable except for the presence of periorbital, yellow-brown plaques with violaceous borders involving the upper and lower eyelids, bilaterally. There was induration, but no warmth or tenderness, of the periorbital plaques. He first noticed these lesions around the time he was diagnosed with CLL; initially they were more discrete yellow papules that developed into plaques over time. They are completely asymptomatic.

A healthy 16-year-old girl presents with six tan patches on her trunk and upper arms, freckles in her axillae, and a reddish discoloration under the tip of her thumbnail. The tan patches have been present since birth but have enlarged over the past 4 years. She reports paroxysmal pain and cold sensitivity involving the discolored portion of her thumb. Examination reveals six tan-brown macules with smooth borders ranging from 16 to 20 mm, axillary freckling, and a tender red-blue nodule under the thumbnail.

A healthy 15-year-old girl presents with a solitary, asymptomatic lesion on her back. The lesion has been present since birth but has enlarged over the past 2 years. She denies association with previous trauma and irritation. Examination reveals multiple, comedo-like openings filled with dark lamellate keratinocyte plugs grouped in a linear distribution over a slightly hypotrophic area of 3 cm by 7 cm. Dermoscopy revealed numerous circular and barrel-shaped homogenous areas in dark-brown shades with remarkable keratin plugs.

A healthy 12-month-old infant girl presents with a yellowish-orange papule on the right upper extremity. Her mother first noticed this lesion approximately 6 months earlier. It has never bled, ulcerated, or formed blisters. The infant does not scratch the lesion nor appears otherwise bothered by it. However, when the lesion is rubbed, it appears to swell and turn bright red. On physical examination, there is a soft, oval-shaped, yellowish papule with a peripheral rim of erythema on the right extensor forearm.

An otherwise healthy 60-year-old dishwasher presents with asymptomatic green discoloration of his right middle fingernail over a period of 2 months. The discoloration began from the distal margin. He denies wearing gloves while working and reports a tendency to pick at his nails when nervous. On examination, distal onycholysis and green discoloration are present exclusively on the right middle nail plate starting from the distal edge without signs of paronychia. Dermoscopy reveals pigment localization under the nail plate.

A 43-year-old elementary school teacher presents with a rash that began on his left thigh approximately 4 months earlier; the rash has since spread. It is mildly itchy but has no associated pain or bleeding. His past medical history is significant for allergic rhinitis and atopic dermatitis. Suspecting eczema, he has been applying an over-the-counter hydrocortisone 1% cream as well as a moisturizer, which transiently alleviates the itch. He has not changed laundry or hygiene products. On physical examination, there are slightly erythematous, minimally scaly patches scattered over his left hip and buttock.

A 50-year-old woman presents with a 5-day history of progressive, painful rash involving her face, trunk, extremities, nasal tip, and ears, in addition to fever and arthralgia. She admits to a history of polysubstance use and states that her last use was a week prior to symptom onset. She denies a history of autoimmune disease or recent travel. Examination reveals retiform purpura with areas of necrosis and bullae formation. Urine toxicology screening is positive for cocaine, and laboratory findings include leukopenia and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (70 mm/h).

A 64-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of a slowly enlarging bump near her left eyebrow. The patient says it appeared suddenly and became a nuisance, as well as cosmetically unacceptable as it enlarged. She denies any pain, tenderness, or oozing, and denies any other similar lesions elsewhere. Her pertinent dermatologic medical and family history are unremarkable. Physical examination reveals a 6-mm nontender subcutaneous mobile nodule on the left lateral eyebrow. There is no overlying ulceration or central punctum, and no discharge is noted. No other suspicious lesions are observed on examination of the scalp and face, aside from mild actinic damage.

A 30-year-old Hispanic woman presents with her 1-year-old son, concerned that he has only small amounts of thin, wispy hair on his head and has none anywhere else on his body. She notes that he does not yet have any teeth, but has a large forehead and ears. He has been irritable and crying for the past day. She reveals a personal history of very high body temperature at times during the summer and says she customarily stays indoors with the air conditioning on, especially in the summer. On physical examination, she has sparse hair on her scalp and eyebrows, as well as eczematous patches on her bilateral lower extremities.

A 25-year-old man with no remarkable past medical history presents with an itchy rash on the feet. Symptoms began 2 months ago, starting over the dorsal toes with redness, scaling, and itching. The eruption spread over the dorsum of the feet and progressed to weeping and crusting. He reports recently buying new shoes for work as a chef, which requires 15 hours daily of standing. Due to profuse sweating, his socks become soaked daily. Examination reveals symmetric erythematous plaques over the bilateral dorsum of both feet with fissures, scaling, and lichenification. No blisters or vesicles are present, but there are scattered crusted erosions.

A 55-year-old black man presents for evaluation of fine wrinkles that had developed over the past year. Physical examination reveals diffuse areas offine wrinkling that run parallel to lines of cleavage on his neck, chest, axilla, trunk, back, and upper arms bilaterally. The affected skin has normal pigmentation and lacks erythema, induration, and atrophy. Lateral tension obliterates the wrinkling. The patient never notes any inflammation, itching, or pain. There are no signs or symptoms of systemic involvement. He denies sunbathing and denies any history of skin disorders or other significant health problems.

A 26-year-old African American man with no significant past medical history presents with a growth on his left foot that had been increasing in size for 1 year. He initially thought it was a wart but had concerns when it continued to grow and became painful. Examination reveals an exophytic, brown, and mildly tender nodule, 3cm in diameter, on his left medial heel and instep. The overlying skin is crusted and friable. His nails and hair show no abnormalities. There is no associated lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the examination is unremarkable.

An African American woman, aged 50 years, presents with painless “bruises” on her leg. She first noticed bruises on both legs a year ago and reports that they have since become larger. Physical examination reveals blue-black macules and patches on both shins. The macules are asymptomatic, and the remainder of the physical examination is within normal limits. A venous stasis ulcer is seen on her right leg. She says she has a 10-year history of discoid and systemic lupus erythematosus treated with hydroxychloroquine and does not recall any history of trauma to her legs.

A man, aged 68 years, with no known history of atopy presents with a 4-month history of an itchy and burning rash on the legs that has been recurring every winter for the past 3 years. He notes that he had dry skin at baseline and did not use emollients, but he did try hydrocortisone 1% cream without improvement. Examination revealed ovoid, erythematous, well-marginated plaques on the lower legs and dorsal feet with variable scaling and focal weeping and crusting. There were no nail changes, and the rest of his skin examination was notable only for xerosis.

An elderly man presents with asymptomatic hyperpigmented, confluent, brown macules on his upper and lower lips, along with hyperpigmented macules on his hands. He also has diffuse blue-black bilateral melanonychia with nail dystrophy on his toenails, and his fingernails contain longitudinal melanonychia with hyperpigmentation of the proximal nail beds. He denies any family history of mucocutaneous pigmentation or gastrointestinal or systemic symptoms. In the last 5 years, results of a colonoscopy, upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, and blood work have all been within normal limits.

A man, aged 42 years, presents with a 6-month history of a painful, scaly skin rash. The eruption is symmetrically distributed over photosensitive areas, affecting his face, neck, upper back, forearms, and hands. The dorsal surfaces of his hands and forearms exhibit a dusky brown coloration over rough and cracked skin. He complains of itching and burning and reports intermittent vomiting and diarrhea. He admits to heavy alcohol intake for the last 2 decades and denies taking any medications. Neuropsychiatric evaluation reveals short-term memory loss, speech problems, and poor concentration.

A 50-year-old woman presents with darkening skin that started several weeks ago. She recently went to the beach and developed severe redness in sun-exposed areas within a few hours of being out in the sun. She did not wear sunscreen and says she usually does not burn in the sun. The affected areas have since darkened. She started hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension 4 months ago. On physical examination, hyperpigmentation is noted on the dorsal hands, proximal forearms, dorsal feet with sparing of skin covered by her sandal straps, “V” of her neck, cheeks, and forehead.

A 61-year-old woman presents with a 7-month history of a bump on the front of her left knee. The lesion is slightly tender but otherwise is asymptomatic. She is concerned that the lesion may be cancerous. She has no other medical problems and takes vitamin D daily. On physical examination, a firm subcutaneous tumor is noted on the left knee measuring 8 cm without overlying skin changes. She has no other similar lesions elsewhere on her body.

A 65-year-old man presents with a recurring rash on his back. He has had the rash several times before, most often during the summer, and it was treated successfully with an antifungal shampoo prescribed by a prior dermatologist. The rash is not itchy or painful. He has a history of depression and hypertension. On physical examination, hyperpigmented macules coalescing into patches with very fine white scale are found. The lesions are scattered primarily on his upper chest and upper back.

A 22-year-old woman presents for evaluation of progressive skin changes on her neck and arms beginning sometime around puberty. She tried various over-the-counter anti-itch, antiaging, and eczema creams that were ineffective. She has no personal or family history of skin conditions and is otherwise healthy. Review of systems is negative for skin laxity, joint hypermobility, or vision changes. Physical examination reveals numerous nontender, noninflammatory, yellow, 2- to 5-mm papules that coalesce into reticulated plaques on the nape of her neck and bilateral antecubital fossa. A punch biopsy demonstrates fragmentation and calcification of elastic fibers.

A 47-year-old otherwise healthy woman presents to the clinic with several concerns. Over the past several months, she has experienced thickening of her skin around her hands, forearms, and face. Her fingers turn blue and then pale when she is exposed to cold. Additional recent symptoms include fatigue and gastroesophageal reflux. She takes no medications and has no family history of autoimmune disease. On physical examination, the patient has skin thickening on the hands, forearms, and face. She also has hypopigmented macules on the hands and lower legs.

A 15-year-old Black man presents with a 1-year history of light spots on his back. The rash has grown slowly, with several new lesions appearing near the first one. It is not itchy or painful. He has not tried any treatments for this condition. He has no relevant medical history and none of his family members have similar skin findings. On examination, there are several well-demarcated depigmented macules and patches on his lateral back.

A 60-year-old Black woman presents with a 30-day history of a nonitchy rash. The rash is located on her face, trunk, and extremities. She reports that she has tried topical steroids on the rash, which did not help. The patient has no other medical conditions and takes no medications. She notes that she had unprotected sex with a new partner about 4 months prior to presentation. On physical examination, the patient has many scattered erythematous scaly papules on her face, abdomen, back, and upper and lower extremities including the palms and soles.

A 64-year-old man with a history of numerous nonmelanoma skin cancers presents with a lesion on the left side of his nose that was first noticed about 6 months ago and is slowly growing. The lesion is not painful or itchy. The patient has not tried any medications on the lesion. The patient wears eyeglasses and the nose pad of his eyeglasses rubs on the lesion. On physical examination, an erythematous papule is found on the left superior nasal sidewall with a central depression.

A 54-year-old woman with a history of depression presents to the clinic with a 1-year history of an intermittent rash. She was hospitalized for COVID-19 approximately 1 year ago and soon after developed a rash all over her body. The lesions persist for several days and have a burning sensation. The patient has no associated joint pain or other systemic symptoms. She tried antihistamines for the rash with no symptomatic relief. On examination, erythematous wheals are evident on her arms and legs as well as her back and abdomen.

A 42-year-old Hispanic man with no prior medical history presents with a 2-month history of a rash on his face, chest, and arms. He reports that the rash gets worse after sun exposure and he has associated joint pain. He has taken over-the-counter nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for the joint pain and topical steroids for the rash with no symptomatic relief. Physical examination reveals erythematous patches over the malar cheeks and dorsal nose sparing the nasolabial fold and erythematous macules on the forearms and chest.

A 6-year-old girl presents with a 1-year history of a waxing and waning rash on her limbs and face. The rash starts as red scaly bumps that fade over several weeks leaving smooth white spots. Every few months, the patient gets several new red bumps. The rash is not itchy or painful. Her parents have tried topical steroid creams that did not help clear the rash. Examination reveals scattered erythematous scaly papules on both legs and several hypopigmented macules on her legs, arms, and face.

A 15-year-old girl presents with patches of hair loss on her scalp that have been present for the last 6 months. She reports that her scalp is not itchy or painful and denies any recent illnesses, diet changes, or stressful life events. She does not have any other medical conditions and takes no medications. Her uncle had a similar condition that started when he was in his 20s, but no one else in the family has experienced hair loss. The patient says she has not tried any treatments for the condition. On examination, she has several well-demarcated patches of hair loss on her frontal and parietal scalp, with no perifollicular erythema or scale.

A 65-year-old man of Middle Eastern descent presents with a tender, weeping mass on his right palm. Since appearing 8 months ago, the lesion has enlarged into a 0.9-cm, pink pedunculated nodule with abundant serous crust. The patient has no significant history of trauma. His medical history is significant for atrial fibrillation, hypertension, coronary artery disease, congestive heart failure, and lung cancer, which was treated with right lobectomy. It is unclear what medications were used to treat his lung cancer. His current medications include metoprolol, lisinopril, allopurinol, aspirin, and digoxin. The patient also presents with additional pink, scaly plaques on his right ankle, consistent with nummular eczema.

A 33-year-old Black man presents to a dermatology clinic with a 5-month history of asymptomatic lesions on his arms and trunk. He is otherwise healthy with no personal or family history of skin disease. He has no history of fever, cough, shortness of breath, or joint pain. The patient has not tried any treatments for these lesions. On examination, there are several smooth, well-demarcated hypopigmented plaques on his upper arms and left flank. He has no similar lesions elsewhere on his body.

A 61-year-old man presents with a 7-month history of lesions on his hands and arms. His medical history includes depression, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. He has no personal or family history of skin problems. His skin lesions are not painful or itchy, and he is not bothered by their appearance. He has not tried any treatments for the lesions. Physical examination reveals a number of pink, annular plaques with smooth raised borders on the patient’s dorsal forearms and hands. On close inspection, small discrete papules are seen within the plaques.

A 32-year-old woman presents with an itchy rash that began 3 months ago. She has a history of anxiety but otherwise no known medical conditions. She has tried over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream to treat the rash, finding some relief from the itchiness, but the rash continues to spread. She has no known allergies and has not changed her skin care products or medications. On examination, the patient has dark purple and gray flat-topped papules with fine gray-white streaks on her flexural wrists, dorsal hands, elbows, ankles, and dorsal feet.

A 35-year-old woman presents to the dermatology clinic with inflammation of her fingernails that first appeared 5 months ago and recently worsened. She reports wearing acrylic nails for the last year, removing them just before the clinic visit. On examination, the patient has erythema and swelling of the lateral nail folds and hyperpigmentation of the proximal nail folds of all fingers on her right hand. Examination also reveals nail dystrophy, onycholysis, and an absence of cuticles. She has not tried any treatments for this condition.

A 42-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital for complications related to type 2 diabetes. Her inpatient team noticed that her right fifth finger was swollen, red, and appeared to have a fissure. The patient stated that although the fissure was not present since birth, her finger has looked this way for “a while” and typically did not bother her. On examination, she had hyperkeratotic plaques on some of her fingers. She denied trauma to the site of injury and her family and travel history were unremarkable.

A 50-year-old woman presents with a crop of lesions that recently appeared on her buttocks and legs. On examination, the red macules and papules range in size from a few millimeters to a few centimeters; when pressed, the lesions do not blanch or partially blanch. The patient reports joint pain over her ankles and knees, along with malaise. When questioned, she acknowledges having had a “cold” a few weeks earlier, for which her primary care provider prescribed an antibiotic. Direct immunofluorescence of the lesions reveals immunoglobulin A (IgA) deposits around the small vessels in the papillary dermis.

A 70-year-old White man presents for evaluation of a recent foot injury. The patient states that he hit his foot at home and noticed blood on the floor; because of a previous injury, he was unable to view his sole. A large (several cm), irregularly shaped plaque is seen on the mid-anterior volar foot. The lesion is brown and black, with central red discoloration and overlying yellow-white scale.

A 35-year-old construction worker presents with a well-circumscribed, verrucous plaque on his left upper arm. The lesion has been present for a few months, but recently has increased in size and become painful. He reports that a cough preceded his skin lesion, but otherwise has no relevant medical history. A large verrucous and ulcerating lesion with pustules is seen. On palpation, a purulent discharge is expressed.

A 45-year-old woman presents with enlarging blood vessels on her tongue that recently have increased in size and number. Numerous 1- to 2-mm discrete red macules and papules are seen on her tongue, oral mucosa, nose, lower lip, and fingertips. She has had frequent nosebleeds since childhood as well as iron-deficiency anemia that has not responded to iron supplementation. Her father, who died at the age of 50, had similar symptoms.

A 12-year-old boy presents to the dermatology clinic with a 2-year history of a brown patch on his chest. The 8-cm patch had been asymptomatic, but over the past 6 months, it has become darker, with hair and acne vulgaris developing within the lesion. The patient is self-conscious about the lesion’s appearance and wishes to learn if it can be treated to lessen the hyperpigmentation.

A 28-year-old Black man presents with a 2-year history of dyspigmentation of his back and chest.
