A 19-year-old college student is brought to the emergency department by their roommates after being found unconscious on their dorm room floor. Their temperature is 102.0°F (38.9°C) and blood pressure is 85/64 mmHg. On physical examination, they have multiple rose-colored spots on the skin covering their abdomen and lower limbs. Lab tests reveal hyperkalemia and an arterial blood gas test that reads pH: 7.04, pCO2: 30.1 mmHg, pO2: 23.4 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient’s condition?

A 17-year-old patient is brought to the emergency room for severe right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain for the past 5 hours. They deny any precipitating events and report a sharp, 8/10, constant pain at the RUQ. They deny any past episodes. Their past medical history is unremarkable, and they are up to date on their vaccinations. Their mother reports a “blood disease” on their father’s side. Their temperature is 101.0°F (38.3°C), blood pressure is 118/70 mmHg, pulse is 103/min, respirations are 18/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. A 45 year old construction worker complains of several weeks of diffuse abdominal pain, constipation, generalized fatigue and irritability. Their vital signs are normal. On examination you notice some distal extremity weakness and thin, a grey-blue line visible along the margin of the gums (Figure A). Red blood cells demonstrate microcytosis, hypochromasia and basophilic with visible dots (Figure B). What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 14-year-old patient is brought to your psychiatric clinic after they were caught stealing their peers’ belongings multiple times by their teacher. A 14-year-old previously healthy patient presents to your office with complaints of two months of dull, aching pain in their right leg that has recently become worse. Though an avid soccer player, they have been unable to participate this season due to the pain and difficulty running. A 32-year-old Caucasian patient presents with a three-month history of weight loss, anxiety, and tremors. They recall frequent heart palpitations and new discomfort while being outside in the heat. Their labs include a TSH level of 0.1 mIU/L. Additionally, the patient’s serum is positive for antibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor. What process is unique to this patient’s diagnosis?

An 85-year-old patient presents to their primary care provider after feeling "lightheaded." Cardiac exam reveals crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur. What is the most likely cause of this patient's diagnosis?

They described that the patient recently lost their house and got divorced within the same week although they seemed fine three days ago. Their labs returned normal and within three days, they appeared normal, had no recollection of the past several days, and discussed in detail how stressful the past two weeks of their life were. They were discharged the next day. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnosis for this patient?

Patient message:
I've been experiencing shortness of breath and a persistent cough for the past week. I tried using my inhaler, but it doesn't seem to help. Should I be concerned about my symptoms? Do I need to schedule an appointment with you?

A 51-year-old white woman presents to the clinic with a 2-year history of a painful, recurrent rash on her fingers. She initially noticed redness, irritation, and pustules around her nails that she thought were caused by an infection. However, the rash progressed to affect the nail bed, eventually destroying her nails. On examination, well-demarcated, scaly plaques with associated pustules and nail atrophy are present on the right second and third distal digits. She is otherwise healthy.

An 8-year-old female child is brought to the clinic for the third time in 4 months presenting with red-brown papules with an overlying mica-like scale on the ventral side of her arms and legs. Her medical and family histories are otherwise unremarkable. Her father states that when the macules and papules go away, the skin where the lesions were previously located is typically lighter than before.

A 24-year-old white male graduate student presents with erythematous, papulopustular patches of skin in a muzzle-like distribution surrounding the mouth, chin, and glabellar region. The lesions are tender to palpation, associated with a stinging and burning sensation, and are aggravated by exfoliating facial washes. Two-year treatment history includes a variety of topical antibiotics, azelaic acid cream, retinoid agents, benzoyl peroxide preparations, topical corticosteroids, and oral tetracycline for cyclic recurrences of outbreaks. These treatment methods were previously successful with complete resolution of each outbreak; however, at present the lesions are persisting despite treatment.

A 20-year-old man presents to the clinic with a circular hypopigmented lesion on his right cheek. The patient stated that he used to have a mole in the same location. Over time he noticed a white area around the mole that enlarged to the current size of the lesion. After a few months he noticed the mole in the center of the lesion had disappeared. On further questioning, he denies any personal or family history of skin cancer.

A 29-year-old man with a history of acne presents to the clinic with 3 discrete, atrophic, blue-tinged plaques on his face. The plaques were located on his forehead and cheeks bilaterally. The patient states the lesions had been present for several months and had slowly worsened until they stabilized at their current appearance. The patient reported that the lesions occurred after he went to a physician for “acne treatment.” The patient has no other medical conditions or relevant social history.

A 22-year-old man complains of an itchy rash on his leg for 4 weeks. He is a collegiate swimmer and had a prior ringworm infection during his freshman year. He has been using over-the-counter antifungal cream for the past 3 weeks with no relief. Multiple round, erythematous, scaling lesions are present on his right leg, some of which are vesicular and weeping. Potassium hydroxide (KOH) test is negative for a dermatophytic infection.

A 62-year-old African American woman presents to establish care and to undergo skin examination, which she reports receiving regularly since her sister was diagnosed with melanoma. Examination reveals 3-mm hyperpigmented horizontal bands across the nailbeds of all fingernails, which she reports have been present since her 20s. She denies experiencing any other nail changes or pain. She takes no medications, and she has no history of skin cancer or suspicious moles. She has no relevant medical history.

A 60-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a 1-cm long horn-like projection coming from the skin on the superior aspect of the skull just lateral to midline. The structure is yellowish-white in color and feels very firm to the touch. She states that she noticed a small, hard lesion a few months ago and that it has grown progressively larger from the time of initial presentation to now. The patient denies any pain at rest but states that she experiences pain when the lesion is struck accidentally.

A 20-year-old female with a medical history of diabetes mellitus type 1 presents with ecchymosis and bullous lesions on her back, posterior legs, and buttocks. She was playing football when she ran into another player and became unconscious. She was immobile in the hospital for 3 days before she regained consciousness. She has about 7 tense blisters with areas of surrounding erythema on the back, buttocks, and posterior thighs.

A 6-year-old Caucasian girl is brought to the clinic by her parents for dry, scaly skin that has persisted for the past 2 years despite the use of commercial moisturizers. Her scaly skin is especially notable over her lower extremities, back, and elbows. The patient denies any pain over the affected areas and reports only a mild itch that is soothed with cold water or lotions. The parents report that she had a similar condition as an infant throughout her entire body and that she has siblings who also have persistently dry skin. Her parents have tried exfoliating the scales with moderate success, but the scales recur shortly thereafter.

A 7-year-old healthy girl is brought to the dermatology clinic by her parents after having had a 3-week history of a rash. The patient’s rash was slightly pruritic, and it involved predominantly the trunk, starting as one larger pink patch with fine scale and subsequently spreading with smaller similar macules and patches. The girl’s palms and soles were spared of the rash.

A 15-month-old girl presents with a history of skin blistering since birth, primarily on her hands, feet, and the perioral face. Blisters and erosions also involve the trunk, some in an annular configuration. There is no family history of neonatal blistering or skin fragility. Over time, the patient has had a decreased number of new vesicles and bullae associated with trauma and friction but has developed thicker skin on the soles of the feet and dystrophic nails.

A 71-year-old Caucasian woman with myelodysplastic syndrome and on chemotherapy with azacitidine presented to the hospital with 2 days of high fever and 4 days of worsening skin lesions. The lesions appeared on the elbows as “blood blisters,” which grew larger and more painful. She denied any other new medications. She was placed on broad spectrum antibiotics by infectious disease physicians out of concern for ecthyma gangrenosum, and dermatology was consulted. On examination, violaceous, edematous plaques with a central pseudovesicle were seen on the bilateral elbows. Punch biopsies were performed for tissue culture and histology.

A 37-year-old woman without a significant past medical history presents to the dermatology clinic with an itchy rash on her right hand that she has had for about 4 months. She had tried numerous over-the-counter hand creams and hydrocortisone cream with no improvement. Additional questioning revealed a 1-year-history of dry, itchy feet. As a construction worker, she wears occlusive, steel-toed work boots and often wears gloves. She is also right-handed. Examination of her hands reveals a normal left hand and a scaly right palm. Diffuse, fine, dry white scale was present on the plantar aspect of both feet.

The patient is a 46-year-old man who presents at your primary care office for an examination with a single lesion that appears on his left arm. During the examination, it is revealed that the patient has a large sclerotic, indurated, hyperpigmented, anhidrotic, and hairless plaque on the right dorsal forearm. The patient states that these lesions had previously been slightly pink for several months before they had turned brown in color and had become “hard.” The patient has type 2 diabetes, but he has no other medical problems. In addition, he has no relevant social or family history.

The patient is a 21-year-old female who presents for continued acne therapy. She has had severe acne on her face, chest, and back for years. She is happy with her current acne regimen of topical tretinoin, topical clindamycin, and oral minocycline. She has been on the regimen for years. On examination, you notice significant blue-black discoloration confined to sites of previous acne scars. The patient has no other medical problems and no relevant social or family history.

A 53-year-old man presents with a rash on his left lower extremity that has been present for several weeks. The patient is a native of Brazil and immigrated to the United States in the past month. He states that the rash is painless and does not itch. On examination, the patient has multiple, raised, hyperpigmented papules on the left lower extremity. There is a large, atrophic, hypopigmented patch on his lower shin, at the site of a previous large ulcer. The superior lesion is the newest, and is beginning to ulcerate. He has no other medical problems.

A 6-month-old infant presents with 2 weeks duration of erythematous papules on the soles of both feet and in the toe web spaces. On examination, a single burrow is visible on the left sole. Multiple family members also complain of a pruritic rash that has been bothering them for several months. The family members have tried multiple over-the-counter creams and remedies without success. The patient has no other medical problems or relevant family history.

A 42-year-old woman presents with a four-day history of experiencing headache, malaise, and stabbing right-sided headache. Two days after her initial symptoms appeared, she developed a rash over the area of pain. She reports that she went hiking through the Texas hill country prior to becoming ill. The patient is otherwise in good health and has an unremarkable medical history. Physical examination reveals unilateral erythematous, thin, raised plaques over the right forehead. In addition, she has no relevant social or family history.

The patient is a 12-year-old Hispanic boy who presents with a 6-month history of nail dystrophy involving all of his fingernails. On examination, all 10 of his fingernails exhibit longitudinal ridging, pitting, fragility, thinning, and distal notching. The patient’s mother is very concerned about the cosmesis of her son’s nails. The patient has no systemic symptoms. On review of systems, the patient’s mother noted that her son has started to develop circular patches of hair loss that appear to resolve on their own. The patient has no relevant social or family history and does not take any medications.

A 1-year-old girl presents with a single, L-shaped, yellow-orange hairless patch over the left preauricular skin. The patient’s father notes that she has never grown hair in that location. The father is concerned because the area used to be smooth, but seems to be changing. The patient has a history of prematurity and low birthweight but is otherwise healthy. The patient has no relevant social or family history.

A 8-year-old African-American girl presents with a 3-day history of fever, pain, and a rash on her trunk. On examination, the patient has several fragile, bullous lesions on her trunk, many of which have eroded, exposing erythematous, annular lesions. The patient is febrile and shaking in the office, and she appears to be in pain. She has no other relevant social or family history and does not take any medications. Her father is very concerned about his daughter.

A 13-year-old girl presents to the dermatology clinic concerned about the development of red, itchy, and sometimes painful bumps on her fingers. She first noted seeing the lesions 2 months prior, in early December. Although the initial lesions have since resolved, new lesions appeared after a skiing trip the previous weekend. The patient is otherwise healthy, with no significant past medical history, and she does not take any medications. Physical examination reveals erythematous, tender papules on the lateral and dorsal aspects of the distal fingers.

A 52-year-old Hispanic man presents with a 3-year history of a very pruritic rash over his shins bilaterally. On examination, both shins are covered in hyperpigmented papules that have coalesced to form thin, rippled plaques. The patient is very concerned about the appearance of his legs and the intense pruritus in the areas of the rash. The patient has no other medical problems and has no systemic symptoms. He has no relevant social or family history and does not take any medications.

The patient is a 13-year-old adolescent boy who presents with a 1-month history of a dark lesion on his finger. He states that the lesion does not bother him, but he came to the clinician because his mother was very concerned about the enlarging area of hyperpigmentation. The patient has no past medical history, no relevant family or social history, and is otherwise in good health. On examination, the rash appears to be a 1 x 1 cm circular patch of hyperpigmentation with overlying scale on the middle finger. During the past month, the rash has grown in size but remains asymptomatic.

A 72-year-old woman presents to the clinic with an intensely itchy rash on her abdomen and chest that appeared 2 months prior. She denies starting any new medications prior to the onset of the eruption and any systemic symptoms. Although she traveled and stayed in hotels recently, she reports that her husband does not exhibit any similar symptoms. Physical examination reveals numerous discrete papules, crusted papules, and papulovesicles on the chest, abdomen, and mid-back. Her upper and lower extremities, face, and groin are unaffected.

The patient is a 38-year-old Hispanic man who presents with a 1-year history of a very pruritic rash over his interscapular area. On examination, he has a circular area of slightly hyperpigmented macules in the interscapular region. The patient complains of pruritus but no pain in the area of the rash. The patient has no other medical problems and has no systemic symptoms. He has no relevant social or family history and does not take any medications.

The patient is a 19-year-old man who presents with several years of a worsening rash. The rash appears as erythematous, hyperkeratotic thin plaques in a seborrheic distribution. The patient states that the rash is very irritating and sometimes pruritic. The patient’s main complaint is that the rash exudes a malodor. The patient states that his father has a similar rash that he chooses not to treat.

A 35-year-old man is referred for evaluation and management of a rash involving both axillae. He reports recurring episodes of the same rash beginning in his early 20s. Lesions develop and involute spontaneously. Areas affected included the axillae, neck, and groin. Historically, outbreaks are more common and worse during the summer, and after vigorous exercise. Both his father and brother have the same problem; his brother saw a specialist, but forgot what he was told. Otherwise, he is healthy and taking no medications. Examination reveals moist, red, crusted, and malodorous plaques with fissures in both axillae.

A 44-year-old man presents for his annual full skin examination. He has a specific concern regarding a lesion on his left lower leg. He recalls having a mosquito bite in that area a few years earlier, but it never went away. The lesion is bothersome only when he shaves his legs and nicks it; otherwise, there is no associated pain or tenderness. Physical examination reveals a firm, flat, pink and brown nodule located on the left anterior proximal shin. The lesion dimples inward when pressure is applied.

A 56-year-old woman presents with diffuse pruritic papules involving the upper body, with nose and forehead thickening. Over the past 2 years, she has been evaluated by multiple specialists for dysphagia, reflux, chronic kidney disease, hypertension, and dyspnea on exertion. Examination results are significant for generalized firm, fleshy, dome-shaped papules of several millimeters in diameter, on her forehead, ears, neck, trunk, back, proximal upper extremities, and dorsal hands, with forehead, glabella, and nose induration. Relevant laboratory findings include monoclonal gammopathy on serum immunofixation, consisting of immunoglobulin (Ig) G_ and IgA_, and unremarkable thyroid panel findings.

A 34-year-old woman presents with an itchy rash, primarily on her arms, but also, to a lesser extent, on her face. She denies any fever or malaise, and her medical history is unremarkable. She does not take any medications and notes that she spent the previous weekend doing yardwork on her property, and the rash appeared 4 days later. Physical examination reveals several linear arrangements of papulovesicles on the dorsal and ventral aspects of her forearms with surrounding erythema.

A 62-year-old white woman with a past medical history of latent tuberculosis, vitiligo, and psoriasis presents for follow-up for treatment of psoriasis. The patient’s psoriasis has proven refractory to numerous treatments over the years, so she began treatment with secukinumab, a monoclonal antibody against interleukin-17A. After 2 months of therapy, the patient reports new-onset tongue pain. Physical examination demonstrates an erythematous, edematous, diamond-shaped plaque on the posterior dorsum of the patient’s tongue.

A 13-month-old toddler with spreading eczema on her trunk and arms is brought in by her father. He is applying moisturizer and a cortisone cream. However, 2 days earlier, a wound appeared on her left hand that appears to be infected. Since then, more areas of raw, oozing skin have developed. Examination reveals lichenified scaling plaques scattered on the trunk and posterior knees and arms, and her left arm has monomorphic crusted vesicles and ulcerations on an erythematous base.

A 30-year-old healthy Hispanic man presents with a slowly progressive facial deformity present since early childhood. He denies any new lesions during this time, any history of trauma to the area, and any family history of similar skin lesions. Examination reveals a bulging, deformed dermal mass with a “bag-of-worms” appearance involving the upper right quadrant of his face, with hypertrophy of the overlying skin and soft tissues. Neurofibromas and café-au-lait macules are not observed.

A healthy 45-year-old man presents with a several-month history of a small papule at the corner of his right eye. The lesion is asymptomatic and is not enlarging, but he has cosmetic concerns. He denies diplopia, vision loss, or any other lesions on his face and body. Examination reveals a dome-shaped, smooth, translucent papule filled with watery fluid located below the lateral canthus of his right eye.

A 32-year-old white man who has never smoked presents with pruritic, tender, erythematous, violaceous patches with eczema-like blisters on his upper, lateral thighs. In 2012, he began traveling annually from Pennsylvania to South Carolina, from January through April, where he works with and rides horses daily from morning to evening. His symptoms began in his first year in South Carolina and appear consistently from January through March. His lesions appear initially in mid-January as a red dot and progress by mid-February. They resolve spontaneously in March.

A healthy 30-year-old woman presents with a 3-year history of an asymptomatic, fleshy papule at the base of her great toe. She denies any new lesions during this time, a history of trauma to the area, or a family history of similar skin lesions. She was treated previously by another dermatologist with cryotherapy; however, she returns to the clinic with recurrence of the lesion. Examination reveals a pedunculated, flesh-colored, well-demarcated tumor on the plantar surface of the base of her great toe.

A 45-year-old man with insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus presents with a sore on his right leg. He describes a long-standing history of asymptomatic lesions on his shins but had only recently injured his leg, causing the sore, which is slow to heal. Despite a 15-year history of diabetes, he has no systemic complications. He has large, well-circumscribed plaques on his anterior shins bilaterally, which are yellow-brown with telangiectasias and minimally violaceous borders.

A 60-year-old woman presents with rapidly growing lesions on her face, trunk, axillae, flexural areas, and groin. The lesions appeared 3 months earlier in her perianal area and extended rapidly to other areas. Previously, she was treated with topical agents for atopic dermatitis and seborrheic dermatitis without improvement. Examination reveals disseminated violaceous papules and plaques on the face, trunk, axillae, and perianal area; some lesions were confluent and ulcerated. Yellowish-red to skin-colored papules are present on the scalp. She has no palpable lymphadenopathy or organomegaly.

A 13-year-old boy presents with a cystic lesion that has been on his forearm for several years. Concerned about the lesion, he reports that it may have grown slightly larger in the past year and it is intermittently painful. More recently, a second similar lesion has appeared in close proximity. He denies any other suspicious lesions elsewhere on his skin. His family history is negative for skin cancer, and he reports no other medical conditions. Physical examination reveals two well-defined 6-mm nodules that are rubbery, slightly tender, and pink on the right proximal ventral forearm. The overlying skin is intact, and there is no associated adenopathy.

A 62-year-old woman with well-controlled rosacea, a monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, and chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL; stable on no current therapy) was seen in the clinic for a full-body skin check. Results of her examination were unremarkable except for the presence of periorbital, yellow-brown plaques with violaceous borders involving the upper and lower eyelids, bilaterally. There was induration, but no warmth or tenderness, of the periorbital plaques. She first noticed these lesions around the time she was diagnosed with CLL; initially they were more discrete yellow papules that developed into plaques over time. They are completely asymptomatic.

A healthy 16-year-old boy presents with six tan patches on his trunk and upper arms, freckles in his axillae, and a reddish discoloration under the tip of his thumbnail. The tan patches have been present since birth but have enlarged over the past 4 years. He reports paroxysmal pain and cold sensitivity involving the discolored portion of his thumb. Examination reveals six tan-brown macules with smooth borders ranging from 16 to 20 mm, axillary freckling, and a tender red-blue nodule under the thumbnail.

A healthy 15-year-old boy presents with a solitary, asymptomatic lesion on his back. The lesion has been present since birth but has enlarged over the past 2 years. He denies association with previous trauma and irritation. Examination reveals multiple, comedo-like openings filled with dark lamellate keratinocyte plugs grouped in a linear distribution over a slightly hypotrophic area of 3 cm by 7 cm. Dermoscopy revealed numerous circular and barrel-shaped homogenous areas in dark-brown shades with remarkable keratin plugs.

A healthy 12-month-old infant boy presents with a yellowish-orange papule on the left upper extremity. His mother first noticed this lesion approximately 6 months earlier. It has never bled, ulcerated, or formed blisters. The infant does not scratch the lesion nor appears otherwise bothered by it. However, when the lesion is rubbed, it appears to swell and turn bright red. On physical examination, there is a soft, oval-shaped, yellowish papule with a peripheral rim of erythema on the right extensor forearm.

An otherwise healthy 60-year-old dishwasher presents with asymptomatic green discoloration of her right middle fingernail over a period of 2 months. The discoloration began from the distal margin. She denies wearing gloves while working and reports a tendency to pick at her nails when nervous. On examination, distal onycholysis and green discoloration are present exclusively on the right middle nail plate starting from the distal edge without signs of paronychia. Dermoscopy reveals pigment localization under the nail plate.

A 43-year-old elementary school teacher presents with a rash that began on her left thigh approximately 4 months earlier; the rash has since spread. It is mildly itchy but has no associated pain or bleeding. Her past medical history is significant for allergic rhinitis and atopic dermatitis. Suspecting eczema, she has been applying an over-the-counter hydrocortisone 1% cream as well as a moisturizer, which transiently alleviates the itch. She has not changed laundry or hygiene products. On physical examination, there are slightly erythematous, minimally scaly patches scattered over her left hip and buttock.

A 50-year-old man presents with a 5-day history of progressive, painful rash involving his face, trunk, extremities, nasal tip, and ears, in addition to fever and arthralgia. He admits to a history of polysubstance use and states that his last use was a week prior to symptom onset. He denies a history of autoimmune disease or recent travel. Examination reveals retiform purpura with areas of necrosis and bullae formation. Urine toxicology screening is positive for cocaine, and laboratory findings include leukopenia and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (70 mm/h).

A 64-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of a slowly enlarging bump near his left eyebrow. The patient says it appeared suddenly and became a nuisance, as well as cosmetically unacceptable as it enlarged. He denies any pain, tenderness, or oozing, and denies any other similar lesions elsewhere. His pertinent dermatologic medical and family history are unremarkable. Physical examination reveals a 6-mm nontender subcutaneous mobile nodule on the left lateral eyebrow. There is no overlying ulceration or central punctum, and no discharge is noted. No other suspicious lesions are observed on examination of the scalp and face, aside from mild actinic damage.

A 30-year-old Hispanic man presents with his 1-year-old daughter, concerned that she has only small amounts of thin, wispy hair on her head and has none anywhere else on her body. He notes that she does not yet have any teeth, but has a large forehead and ears. She has been irritable and crying for the past day. He reveals a personal history of very high body temperature at times during the summer and says he customarily stays indoors with the air conditioning on, especially in the summer. On physical examination, he has sparse hair on his scalp and eyebrows, as well as eczematous patches on his bilateral lower extremities.

A 25-year-old woman with no remarkable past medical history presents with an itchy rash on the feet. Symptoms began 2 months ago, starting over the dorsal toes with redness, scaling, and itching. The eruption spread over the dorsum of the feet and progressed to weeping and crusting. She reports recently buying new shoes for work as a chef, which requires 15 hours daily of standing. Due to profuse sweating, her socks become soaked daily. Examination reveals symmetric erythematous plaques over the bilateral dorsum of both feet with fissures, scaling, and lichenification. No blisters or vesicles are present, but there are scattered crusted erosions.

A 55-year-old black woman presents for evaluation of fine wrinkles that had developed over the past year. Physical examination reveals diffuse areas of fine wrinkling that run parallel to lines of cleavage on her neck, chest, axilla, trunk, back, and upper arms bilaterally. The affected skin has normal pigmentation and lacks erythema, induration, and atrophy. Lateral tension obliterates the wrinkling. The patient never notes any inflammation, itching, or pain. There are no signs or symptoms of systemic involvement. She denies sunbathing and denies any history of skin disorders or other significant health problems.

A 26-year-old African American woman with no significant past medical history presents with a growth on her left foot that had been increasing in size for 1 year. She initially thought it was a wart but had concerns when it continued to grow and became painful. Examination reveals an exophytic, brown, and mildly tender nodule, 3cm in diameter, on her left medial heel and instep. The overlying skin is crusted and friable. Her nails and hair show no abnormalities. There is no associated lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the examination is unremarkable.

An African American man, aged 50 years, presents with painless “bruises” on his leg. He first noticed bruises on both legs a year ago and reports that they have since become larger. Physical examination reveals blue-black macules and patches on both shins. The macules are asymptomatic, and the remainder of the physical examination is within normal limits. A venous stasis ulcer is seen on his right leg. He says he has a 10-year history of discoid and systemic lupus erythematosus treated with hydroxychloroquine and does not recall any history of trauma to his legs.

A woman, aged 68 years, with no known history of atopy presents with a 4-month history of an itchy and burning rash on the legs that has been recurring every winter for the past 3 years. She notes that she had dry skin at baseline and did not use emollients, but she did try hydrocortisone 1% cream without improvement. Examination revealed ovoid, erythematous, well-marginated plaques on the lower legs and dorsal feet with variable scaling and focal weeping and crusting. There were no nail changes, and the rest of her skin examination was notable only for xerosis.

An elderly woman presents with asymptomatic hyperpigmented, confluent, brown macules on her upper and lower lips, along with hyperpigmented macules on her hands. She also has diffuse blue-black bilateral melanonychia with nail dystrophy on her toenails, and her fingernails contain longitudinal melanonychia with hyperpigmentation of the proximal nail beds. She denies any family history of mucocutaneous pigmentation or gastrointestinal or systemic symptoms. In the last 5 years, results of a colonoscopy, upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, and blood work have all been within normal limits.

A woman, aged 42 years, presents with a 6-month history of a painful, scaly skin rash. The eruption is symmetrically distributed over photosensitive areas, affecting her face, neck, upper back, forearms, and hands. The dorsal surfaces of her hands and forearms exhibit a dusky brown coloration over rough and cracked skin. She complains of itching and burning and reports intermittent vomiting and diarrhea. She admits to heavy alcohol intake for the last 2 decades and denies taking any medications. Neuropsychiatric evaluation reveals short-term memory loss, speech problems, and poor concentration.

A 50-year-old man presents with darkening skin that started several weeks ago. He recently went to the beach and developed severe redness in sun-exposed areas within a few hours of being out in the sun. He did not wear sunscreen and says he usually does not burn in the sun. The affected areas have since darkened. He started hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension 4 months ago. On physical examination, hyperpigmentation is noted on the dorsal hands, proximal forearms, dorsal feet with sparing of skin covered by his sandal straps, “V” of his neck, cheeks, and forehead.

A 61-year-old man presents with a 7-month history of a bump on the front of his left knee. The lesion is slightly tender but otherwise is asymptomatic. He is concerned that the lesion may be cancerous. He has no other medical problems and takes vitamin D daily. On physical examination, a firm subcutaneous tumor is noted on the left knee measuring 8 cm without overlying skin changes. He has no other similar lesions elsewhere on his body.

A 65-year-old woman presents with a recurring rash on her back. She has had the rash several times before, most often during the summer, and it was treated successfully with an antifungal shampoo prescribed by a prior dermatologist. The rash is not itchy or painful. She has a history of depression and hypertension. On physical examination, hyperpigmented macules coalescing into patches with very fine white scale are found. The lesions are scattered primarily on her upper chest and upper back.

A 22-year-old man presents for evaluation of progressive skin changes on his neck and arms beginning sometime around puberty. He tried various over-the-counter anti-itch, antiaging, and eczema creams that were ineffective. He has no personal or family history of skin conditions and is otherwise healthy. Review of systems is negative for skin laxity, joint hypermobility, or vision changes. Physical examination reveals numerous nontender, noninflammatory, yellow, 2- to 5-mm papules that coalesce into reticulated plaques on the nape of his neck and bilateral antecubital fossa. A punch biopsy demonstrates fragmentation and calcification of elastic fibers.

A 47-year-old otherwise healthy man presents to the clinic with several concerns. Over the past several months, he has experienced thickening of his skin around his hands, forearms, and face. His fingers turn blue and then pale when he is exposed to cold. Additional recent symptoms include fatigue and gastroesophageal reflux. He takes no medications and has no family history of autoimmune disease. On physical examination, the patient has skin thickening on the hands, forearms, and face. He also has hypopigmented macules on the hands and lower legs.

A 15-year-old Black woman presents with a 1-year history of light spots on her back. The rash has grown slowly, with several new lesions appearing near the first one. It is not itchy or painful. She has not tried any treatments for this condition. She has no relevant medical history and none of her family members have similar skin findings. On examination, there are several well-demarcated depigmented macules and patches on her lateral back.

A 60-year-old Black man presents with a 30-day history of a nonitchy rash. The rash is located on his face, trunk, and extremities. He reports that he has tried topical steroids on the rash, which did not help. The patient has no other medical conditions and takes no medications. He notes that he had unprotected sex with a new partner about 4 months prior to presentation. On physical examination, the patient has many scattered erythematous scaly papules on his face, abdomen, back, and upper and lower extremities including the palms and soles.

A 64-year-old woman with a history of numerous nonmelanoma skin cancers presents with a lesion on the left side of her nose that was first noticed about 6 months ago and is slowly growing. The lesion is not painful or itchy. The patient has not tried any medications on the lesion. The patient wears eyeglasses and the nose pad of her eyeglasses rubs on the lesion. On physical examination, an erythematous papule is found on the left superior nasal sidewall with a central depression.

A 54-year-old man with a history of depression presents to the clinic with a 1-year history of an intermittent rash. He was hospitalized for COVID-19 approximately 1 year ago and soon after developed a rash all over his body. The lesions persist for several days and have a burning sensation. The patient has no associated joint pain or other systemic symptoms. He tried antihistamines for the rash with no symptomatic relief. On examination, erythematous wheals are evident on his arms and legs as well as his back and abdomen.

A 42-year-old Hispanic woman with no prior medical history presents with a 2-month history of a rash on her face, chest, and arms. She reports that the rash gets worse after sun exposure and she has associated joint pain. She has taken over-the-counter nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for the joint pain and topical steroids for the rash with no symptomatic relief. Physical examination reveals erythematous patches over the malar cheeks and dorsal nose sparing the nasolabial fold and erythematous macules on the forearms and chest.

A 6-year-old boy presents with a 1-year history of a waxing and waning rash on his limbs and face. The rash starts as red scaly bumps that fade over several weeks leaving smooth white spots. Every few months, the patient gets several new red bumps. The rash is not itchy or painful. His parents have tried topical steroid creams that did not help clear the rash. Examination reveals scattered erythematous scaly papules on both legs and several hypopigmented macules on his legs, arms, and face.

A 15-year-old boy presents with patches of hair loss on his scalp that have been present for the last 6 months. He reports that his scalp is not itchy or painful and denies any recent illnesses, diet changes, or stressful life events. He does not have any other medical conditions and takes no medications. His aunt had a similar condition that started when she was in her 20s, but no one else in the family has experienced hair loss. The patient says he has not tried any treatments for the condition. On examination, he has several well-demarcated patches of hair loss on his frontal and parietal scalp, with no perifollicular erythema or scale.

A 65-year-old woman of Middle Eastern descent presents with a tender, weeping mass on her right palm. Since appearing 8 months ago, the lesion has enlarged into a 0.9-cm, pink pedunculated nodule with abundant serous crust. The patient has no significant history of trauma. Her medical history is significant for atrial fibrillation, hypertension, coronary artery disease, congestive heart failure, and lung cancer, which was treated with right lobectomy. It is unclear what medications were used to treat her lung cancer. Her current medications include metoprolol, lisinopril, allopurinol, aspirin, and digoxin. The patient also presents with additional pink, scaly plaques on her right ankle, consistent with nummular eczema.

A 33-year-old Black woman presents to a dermatology clinic with a 5-month history of asymptomatic lesions on her arms and trunk. She is otherwise healthy with no personal or family history of skin disease. She has no history of fever, cough, shortness of breath, or joint pain. The patient has not tried any treatments for these lesions. On examination, there are several smooth, well-demarcated hypopigmented plaques on her upper arms and left flank. She has no similar lesions elsewhere on her body.

A 61-year-old woman presents with a 7-month history of lesions on her hands and arms. Her medical history includes depression, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. She has no personal or family history of skin problems. Her skin lesions are not painful or itchy, and she is not bothered by their appearance. She has not tried any treatments for the lesions. Physical examination reveals a number of pink, annular plaques with smooth raised borders on the patient’s dorsal forearms and hands. On close inspection, small discrete papules are seen within the plaques.

A 32-year-old man presents with an itchy rash that began 3 months ago. He has a history of anxiety but otherwise no known medical conditions. He has tried over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream to treat the rash, finding some relief from the itchiness, but the rash continues to spread. He has no known allergies and has not changed his skin care products or medications. On examination, the patient has dark purple and gray flat-topped papules with fine gray-white streaks on his flexural wrists, dorsal hands, elbows, ankles, and dorsal feet.

A 35-year-old man presents to the dermatology clinic with inflammation of his fingernails that first appeared 5 months ago and recently worsened. He reports wearing acrylic nails for the last year, removing them just before the clinic visit. On examination, the patient has erythema and swelling of the lateral nail folds and hyperpigmentation of the proximal nail folds of all fingers on his right hand. Examination also reveals nail dystrophy, onycholysis, and an absence of cuticles. He has not tried any treatments for this condition.

A 42-year-old man was admitted to the hospital for complications related to type 2 diabetes. His inpatient team noticed that his right fifth finger was swollen, red, and appeared to have a fissure. The patient stated that although the fissure was not present since birth, his finger has looked this way for “a while” and typically did not bother him. On examination, he had hyperkeratotic plaques on some of his fingers. He denied trauma to the site of injury and his family and travel history were unremarkable.

A 50-year-old man presents with a crop of lesions that recently appeared on his buttocks and legs. On examination, the red macules and papules range in size from a few millimeters to a few centimeters; when pressed, the lesions do not blanch or partially blanch. The patient reports joint pain over his ankles and knees, along with malaise. When questioned, he acknowledges having had a “cold” a few weeks earlier, for which his primary care provider prescribed an antibiotic. Direct immunofluorescence of the lesions reveals immunoglobulin A (IgA) deposits around the small vessels in the papillary dermis.

A 70-year-old White woman presents for evaluation of a recent foot injury. The patient states that she hit her foot at home and noticed blood on the floor; because of a previous injury, she was unable to view her sole. A large (several cm), irregularly shaped plaque is seen on the mid-anterior volar foot. The lesion is brown and black, with central red discoloration and overlying yellow-white scale.

A 35-year-old construction worker presents with a well-circumscribed, verrucous plaque on her left upper arm. The lesion has been present for a few months, but recently has increased in size and become painful. She reports that a cough preceded her skin lesion, but otherwise has no relevant medical history. A large verrucous and ulcerating lesion with pustules is seen. On palpation, a purulent discharge is expressed.

A 45-year-old man presents with enlarging blood vessels on his tongue that recently have increased in size and number. Numerous 1- to 2-mm discrete red macules and papules are seen on his tongue, oral mucosa, nose, lower lip, and fingertips. He has had frequent nosebleeds since childhood as well as iron-deficiency anemia that has not responded to iron supplementation. His father, who died at the age of 50, had similar symptoms.

A 12-year-old girl presents to the dermatology clinic with a 2-year history of a brown patch on her chest. The 8-cm patch had been asymptomatic, but over the past 6 months, it has become darker, with hair and acne vulgaris developing within the lesion. The patient is self-conscious about the lesion’s appearance and wishes to learn if it can be treated to lessen the hyperpigmentation.

A 28-year-old Black woman presents with a 2-year history of dyspigmentation of her back and chest. The patient notes that the lesions initially had red borders but these have faded over the past several months. Physical examination reveals circular, ashy-gray macules distributed diffusely over her back and chest. The patient denies pain or pruritus and takes no medication. She notes that she recently traveled to Mexico. She has been relatively unconcerned about the lesions and only sought medical care to rule out cancer.

A 45-year-old man presents with oval-shaped lesions on his arms that he first noted a few months ago. The lesions began as an area of discrete erythema, progressed to induration, and then became dark, smooth, and shiny. He has a family history of rheumatoid arthritis. On examination, the patient has multiple hyperpigmented and hypopigmented indurated plaques with a shiny surface; his nails and fingertips are normal, and autoantibody tests were negative.

A 8-year-old girl presents with a 2-month history of an asymptomatic rash on the dorsum of her right hand. She and her family have recently moved from a coastal region in Mexico. Medical and family history are otherwise unremarkable. On examination, she has a 2-cm pigmented macular lesion with an irregular outline centrally located on the dorsal aspect of her right hand. The remainder of the physical examination is normal. Dermoscopy rules out a nevoid lesion, and septated filaments are observed on potassium hydroxide (KOH) test.

A 53-year-old woman presents to the clinic with ulcerated, scarred, and hypertrophic plaques on both lower extremities. She is a refugee from Sudan who arrived in the United States a month earlier. She reports that the lesions started as red bumps that slowly expanded and developed a raised border. Several of her family members in Sudan have had similar lesions in the past, and she is concerned that she may have developed the same condition.

A 48-year-old white woman presents to the dermatology clinic with papulosquamous cutaneous lesions that recently appeared on her chest, arms, and the dorsal aspects of her hands. The patient has a family history of autoimmune disorders, including systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Physical examination reveals that the lesions lack induration and do not appear to be leaving scars. Biopsy of the lesion is performed, revealing mild inflammatory infiltrate. Direct immunofluorescence shows a granular deposition at the dermal-epidermal junction. Serology indicates that the patient is positive for anti-Ro/SSA (Sjögren-syndrome-related antigen A).

A 15-year-old white adolescent presents to the dermatology clinic with an asymptomatic rash on her upper back that has persisted for 4 months. Physical examination reveals hyperpigmented scaly papules coalescing into confluent plaques with peripheral reticulated papillomatosis. The girl is overweight but has no history of any other medical conditions.

A 8-year-old girl presents to the clinic for evaluation of a progressively worsening nail dystrophy that began a few months ago. The patient’s father denies a family history of skin diseases and reports that his daughter has no history of medical problems. On physical examination, all of the girl’s fingernails and toenails show hyperkeratosis, longitudinal ridging, loss of luster, and roughness. Her hair, skin, and oral mucosa are unremarkable. Nail biopsy reveals spongiotic changes and exocytosis of inflammatory cells into the nail epithelia. The results of a fungal culture are negative.

A 54-year-old man presents with 2 years of gradual hair thinning. He says that his mother also experienced hair thinning starting in her 50s. He denies scalp itch. He denies clumps of hair coming out in the shower or on his pillow. He denies any preceding stressful life events. He denies wearing his hair in tight braids. He denies loss of eyebrows or eyelashes.

A 45-year-old man presents with 3 months of tender bumps on the shins. He says that 4 months ago, he was hospitalized for abdominal pain and was found to be positive for hepatitis B. He denies ever having tuberculosis. He denies itching or scratching at the bumps. He denies any rash on the trunk or extremities.

A 70-year-old woman presents with 1 year of a non-healing growth on the right cheek. She says she first noticed it when she accidentally bumped into it and it bled easily. She denies any preceding trauma to the lesion.

An 8-year-old female presents with 1 week of itchy blisters on the ears. She just recently returned from spring break with her family. She denies using any particular products on the ears before the rash. She says that this has occurred yearly for the last several years, always around the same time. She denies proximal muscle weakness. She denies flaking in the scalp.

A 67-year-old female presents with unrelenting itch present over the last 6 months. She endorses weight loss and fatigue. She denies any liver or kidney disease. She denies exacerbation of itch with water. Physical examination is significant for numerous punctate and linear erosions consistent with excoriations as well as diffuse shoddy lymphadenopathy. A KOH scraping is performed which is negative for scabies.

A 25-year-old female presents with 6 months of discoloration in the underarms. She denies any blisters or erosions in the areas. She denies any history of diabetes, insulin resistance, or weight gain. She denies itch. She denies discoloration only with sweating. Physical examination reveals reddish-brown patches in the underarms; Wood's lamp reveals coral red fluorescence.

A 72-year-old man is seen by the Dermatology consult service for a rash which has developed during a prolonged 6-week hospitalization following a hemorrhagic stroke. He is currently intubated, so history is limited, but per chart review, nurses documented the rash starting 5 days ago. He has been experiencing high fevers as well as unexplained transaminitis over the last few days. He has taken atorvastatin and pantoprazole for years, including during the hospitalization. Following the stroke, he was started on carbamazepine for seizure prophylaxis. He contracted MRSA pneumonia 2 weeks ago and has been on vancomycin since then. He has also been on cefepime and micafungin for the last 5 days given the fevers and transaminitis. Physical examination is significant for diffuse erythematous patches extending over the face, chest, back, and extremities, as well as facial edema.

A 25-year-old female presents with 2 years of pruriginous erythematous plaques with silver scales on elbows, knees and buttocks. She says that her father is known for hand and back arthritis. She denies personal and family history of dermatology conditions and atopy. Physical exam reveals pitting on all 10 fingernails.

A 60-year-old male presents with a non-healing painful ulcer on his right leg for 4 months. He says he first noticed it after he accidentally bumped into a chair. He is known for rheumatoid arthritis and hypertension, and has taken methotrexate and bisoprolol for years. According to the patient, oral antibiotics and wound debridement have only increased the size of the ulcer. Physical exam reveals a 5x5 cm fibrinous ulcer with violaceous undermined borders on his right shin.

A 10-year-old female presents with non-blanchable palpable purple papules on both legs for a week. Sore throat preceded the skin lesions. Her parents deny any other history of infectious diseases or new medications. The girl complains about abdominal pain and trouble walking. Her vitals are stable. Physical exam reveals red and swollen ankles on top of palpable purpura on both legs.

A 16-year-old female presents with an increased number of perinasal dome-shaped smooth flesh-colored papules. She is known to have epilepsy. She denies family history of cancer. The physical exam reveals hypopigmented macules on her back, three café-au-lait patches, skin colored to hypopigmented plaque on the trunk, and flesh-colored papules emerging from nail folds. A biopsy of the facial lesions shows dermal proliferation of fibroblasts in a collagenous stroma associated with increased dilated blood vessels.

A 40-year-old male complains about squamous papules on his scalp for 10 years. These lesions responded to topical corticosteroids but recur when the treatment is stopped. He denies any systemic symptoms. Physical exam reveals erythematous scaly papules with signs of atrophy and scarring, as well as cicatricial alopecia. Skin biopsy shows lichenoid interface dermatitis with hyperkeratosis and follicular plugging.

A 30-year-old male presents with itchy skin lesions on his arms and legs. He denies family history of atopy and psoriasis. He does not take any medication and has no risk factors for hepatitis. Review of systems came back negative. Physical exam reveals flat purple papules and plaques on his wrists and shins as well as white plaques with lacy patterns in the oral mucosa.

A 40-year-old male presents with a recurrent skin eruption on his nose and cheeks for 2 years. These lesions appear usually in the summer following excessive sun exposure, and disappear without scarring. He has complaints about arthritis and chronic fatigue. He denies muscle weakness. Physical exam reveals eroded butterfly-shaped erythematous plaques over the malar area, non-scarring alopecia and oral ulcers.

A 22-year-old female presents with a follicular eruption that has been present for 2 weeks. She has a history of anorexia nervosa and alcoholism. There is no identifiable preceding incident related to the eruption. She denies a history of atopy, drug use, and new medications. A review of systems shows positive findings for joint pain and bleeding gums. Physical exam reveals ecchymosis and purpuric follicular papules with corkscrew-like hair on her legs and arms.

A 5-year-old male presents with a plaque on his left leg. The lesion appeared a few months after his birth. It has been increasing in size proportionally to his growth. The parents mention that the skin lesion sometimes becomes irritated, erythematous and itchy when the patient plays with it or when he gets sick. Physical exam reveals a red-brown well delimited plaque on his left leg without any noticeable erythema or epidermal changes.

A 12 year old female presents to clinic with concerns for new red bumps developing on the chest, arms, and legs over the past few months. Patient states the lesions begin as small bumps that slowly grow in size and persist. She denies any pain, itch, or symptoms associated with the lesions. She has not tried any treatment and denies any recent travel. The patient's father states the patient also has a few light brown patches on the body, and some of his other family members had similar spots. The patient is currently receiving extra classes for learning disability, and recently was evaluated by orthopaedics for spinal irregularities. On physical examination, multiple skin colored papules that are able to be pushed in with a finger are spread across the chest, arms, and bilateral lower extremities. Seven light tan-brown ovoid uniform patches are scattered throughout the trunk and legs. The bilateral axilla are noted to have few scattered ovoid tan brown macules.

A 34 year old man presents to clinic complaining of a painful, red spot on the left shoulder that developed about 4 years ago. He denies any trauma that may have incited it. It has been evaluated by multiple dermatologists and treated with intralesional corticosteroid injections, but it continues to enlargen and has become more raised.  Physical examination reveals a multilobular violaceous, poorly demarcated firm plaque that is tender to palpation on the left shoulder. Histopathologic analysis of the lesion reveals lesional cells that stain positive for CD34 and negative for Factor 13a.

A 45-year-old-woman with a past medical history of knee pain and hypertension complains of dark spot on the lower lip and hands that develop whenever she takes certain oral medications. She states the rash has been ongoing for several years, and usually begins as a pink spot with a darker brown-black center. She denies any bleeding or ulceration at the site.  Current medications includes naproxen, multivitamins, and metoprolol.   Physical examination reveals a well demarcated red-purple patch with a darker red-violaceous center on the dorsal hands and lower lip. The patch is non-painful.

A 67-year-old-female farmer presents complaining of a growing mole on the right side of her cheek.   She states the mole was present for several years, but then started growing rapidly on one side a few weeks ago. Sometimes the mole will bleed on its own. She tries to avoid picking at the area.   Physical examination shows tan-brown ovoid irregularly shaped hyperpigmented macule with focal ulceration. Dermoscopy demonstrates a blue-gray veil in the center of the lesion.

A 13-year-old boy presents to the dermatology clinic with a light patch over both elbow creases that the dad noticed a few months ago. The spots have been growing in size. The patient denies any pain at the site, and thinks he may have scraped his arms that caused the light patch.   Physical examination reveals well demarcated depigmented irregularly shaped patches on the bilateral antecubital fossas.

A 45-year-old woman with a past medical history of hypertension presents with concerns of a rash on her left thigh back that her husband noticed two days ago. The rash has been progressively enlargened. Patient denies any pain or any prior treatments. She thinks the surrounding skin is warm and may be infected, but she denies any drainage.  She reports that they went hiking eight days ago in Rhode Island.   Physical exam demonstrates a non-scaly large targetoid, pink-red patch on the left thigh

A 54-year-old female is hospitalized for a left lower leg cellulitis and treated with ampicillin. On day 4 of hospitalization, she developed a rash on the neck, under the arms that start as small yellow bumps but rapidly spread. She denies any new lotions or creams.  She denies any personal or family history of psoriasis.   Physical examination reveals multiple studded monomorphic yellow pustules on erythematous bright pink bases that coalesce into plaques across the flexural neck, bilateral axilla, trunk, and inframmary folds.

A 66-year-old man with a past medical history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus type 2 presents to clinic with a mildly painful, pruritic peeling skin on the chest and back that began 4 weeks ago. He denies any new medications, new topical creams or lotions, or laundry detergents. He has been applying vaseline to the spots. He also thinks he may have a similar spot on the scalp. He denies any similar spots in the mouth, and denies forming any blisters on the skin.   Physical exam demonstrates multiple thinly eroded pink-red oval plaques on the chest, scalp, back with yellow brown corn-flake like scale. Ocular and oral mucosa are normal.

A 21-year-old man presents to clinic with rough, firm spots on both earlobes that developed three months ago when he underwent ear piercings. He has tried over the counter hydrocortisone without any improvement.   He notes that he has a history of multiple similar spots that developed after he injured himself, and multiple family members have similar spots.   On physical exam, thick pink firm plaques are noted at the sites of ear piercings that extend beyond margin of the scar.

A 35-year-old woman with a past medical history of obesity and tobacco use presents to clinic with a seven month history of boils under the arms and in the groin. She reports that the boils come up twice a week under the arms, and once a week in the groin. The individual boils are painful and will often drain foul odorous yellow green material. Many of the boils have been drained in the emergency room.   Physical examination reveals multiple painful, tender subcutaneous nodules draining yellow-white malodorous pus in the bilateral axilla and inguinal folds. Scattered double headed comedones and sinus tracts are present.

A 45-year-old woman presents to the primary care clinic with a red, itchy rash on the eyebrows and around the nose that has been ongoing for eight months. She has tried moisturizers to the areas, but the flakiness returns a few days later. She also reports she has dandruff in her scalp. She denies any new facial products or using any other creams or lotions.   Physical examination reveals greasy yellow scale on poorly demarcated erythematous patches on the eyebrows and bilateral nasal alar creases. Mild white scale is appreciated diffusely across the scalp.

A 24-year-old obese man presents to the dermatology clinic with darkening, rough skin around the neck for six months. The rash is not painful or itchy. He has tried to clean the area with over the counter shampoo and rubbing alcohol without improvement. He denies any rash elsewhere on the body. The rash always begins as dark patches, and he denies any blistering or redness before the dark spots develop.   Physical examination reveals thick, velvety ropey hyperpigmented rough, poorly demarcated plaques circumferentially around the neck.

A 65-year-old African American woman presents to dermatology clinic for multiple non-painful, non-itchy brown spots on the face. She notes they started developing when she was 42 years old, and they have increased in number and size. Sometimes she tries to remove them with a needle, but they will bleed.   Physical exam reveals multiple dark, flat topped ovoid papules, and few pedunculated brown-black papules on the bilateral zygomatic cheeks.

A 5-year-old girl presents to the pediatrician office with complaints of multiple spots that began on the abdomen and spread to the arms and legs. The spots are not itchy or painful, unless she scratches them. Sometimes the skin surrounding the lesion will become very red and painful, but then the lesion and redness fade. The parents report they have tried topical corticosteroids but the lesions do not go away. Dad endorses a history of atopic dermatitis in his brother and himself. Physical exam reveals multiple dome shaped skin colored to light pink papules with central umbilication and yellow core across the chest, abdomen, and back.

A 65-year-old male presents to the dermatology clinic for evaluation of eyelid redness and neck rash ongoing for four months that began after he started a new body lotion. He reports increasing fatigue when climbing stairs and lifting heavy items over his head. He has not tried any topical treatments. He denies any recent medication changes, fevers, chills, or recent travel.   Physical examination reveals poorly demarcated patchy pink erythema affecting the periocular areas with a bright pink poorly demarcated patch diffusely across the upper back and shoulders in the shape of a V. The bilateral dorsal hands reveals thin pink rough plaques on the knuckle joints.

A 53-year-old male with a past medical history of multiple myeloma presents to dermatology clinic with multiple yellow, irritated spots under the eyes. He reports the lesions developed about four months ago, beginning as a red spot that will enlargen, bleed, and then may scab over with yellow material. He denies any new facial creams, topical treatments, or new medications. He does not have any new dogs or cats.   Physical examination is remarkable for hepatosplenomegaly and periocular bilaterally are yellow-pink multilobular papules and plaques.

A 34-year-old man presents with complaints of a severely itchy rash affecting both lower legs that developed three days ago after returning from camping six days ago. He reports during the camping trip they often hiked for several hours a day, and he wore shorts due to the humid, hot weather. When the rash began, it began as small red bumps that formed larger fluid filled bumps. He has tried over the counter cortisone that helps with the itch a little bit. He denies any new topical lotions, laundry detergents, or body washes.   Physical exam reveals multiple streaks of yellow vesicles on bright pink erythematous bases in a linear distribution on the bilateral lower extremities.

A 75-year-old female presents with a few day history of blisters developing on her arms and legs. She denies any exposures to poison ivy, any recent travel, and any recent medication changes. Physical examination demonstrates thin urticarial pink plaques on the abdomen and multiple tense bullae without significant underlying erythema scattered on the arms and legs.

A 2-year-old male with a past medical history of cleft palate presents to clinic with growths on the face. Patient's father reports the growths were noticed at birth, then slowly grew in size over time before stopping. The patient is meeting all developmental milestones otherwise. Examination reveals a skin colored papule immediately in the bilateral pre-auricular areas.

A 23-year-old male presents to urgent clinic with complaints of sunburn. Patient endorses history of traveling to the beach a week ago and did not apply any sunblock. He endorses fevers, but review of systems is otherwise negative. He noticed a facial rash a few days ago that feels warm to touch on the face. Family history is remarkable for similar rash in his mother. He does not take any medications. Physical examination of the face reveals bright pink thin plaques on the bilateral cheeks extending onto the nasal bridge but sparing the nasolabial folds bilaterally.

A 16-year-old female with past medical history of severe nodulocystic acne presents to the emergency room with increasing painful cysts on the trunk after recently starting oral isotretinoin in the past 3 weeks. Patient endorses fevers, chills, joint pain particularly along the chest. Examination reveals multiple inflammatory papules and large cystic nodules with hemorrhagic crust on the chest, shoulders, and back. The sternum is tender to palpation.

A 71-year-old female with a past medical history of poorly controlled diabetes and heart transplant is noted to have fevers and a black eschar on the nose on day 41 of hospitalization in the ICU. The patient is intubated and unable to provide history. Nurses report the area was first noticed to be darker and then rapidly expanded. Review of current medications include cyclosporine, tacrolimus, insulin, and broad spectrum antibiotics. Physical examination reveals an extensive dark black, necrotic eschar on the nasal bridge and left nasal sidewall, cheek, and lip with surrounding pink erythema. Oral examination reveals black eschars on upper palate.

A 5-year-old female with a past medical history of well-controlled eczema presents with light colored patches on the face and forearms noticed by the patient's parents a few days ago. Parents deny any trauma to the sites or any new topical products. Patient denies any pruritus or pain at the affected areas. Examination of the face reveals poorly demarcated ovoid hypopigmented patches on the cheeks and forearms.

A 34-year-old Asian male presents with multiple spots under the eyes growing over the past several years. He denies any associated pain or pruritus. The growths have remained stable in size. He does not take any medications. Examination is remarkable for multiple flat topped thin skin colored papules under the eyes bilaterally.

A 32-year-old female with past medical history of poorly controlled HIV presents to clinic with dark spots on the skin and in the mouth. She cannot recall when they first started. She denies any drug or alcohol use. She is not currently taking her antiretroviral therapy. Examination reveals multiple ovoid violaceous ruddy, brown ovoid macules on the trunk, legs, oral palate and plantar feet. A punch biopsy is performed and stains for HHV-8 is positive.

A 1-year-old female presents with intermittent history of itchy spots on the palms and soles that flare and then resolve over the past 6 months. Father is unable to identify any clear inciting trigger. He has tried over the counter hydrocortisone but lesions remain. An in office mineral oil preparation is negative for any microorganisms. Physical examination reveals vesiculopustules over the palms, soles, and ankles.

A 14-year-old female with history of leukemia treated with chemotherapy underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplant and on day 30 post therapy was noted to have a rash on the trunk that rapidly spread to the hands, feet, ears. Patient was also reported to have fevers, chills, diarrhea and new transaminitis.  Examination remarkable for acral erythema and scattered pink erythematous macules and poorly demarcated papules on the trunk, extremities with prominent follicular erythema.

A 21-year-old female presents to the urgent care clinic after returning from the beach seven days ago. About three days ago, she noticed a red worm like rash on the bottom of her left foot that has been progressively moving. She reports walking barefoot on the beach. Examination reveals a serpiginous red-yellow plaque extending from left plantar forefoot to the medial aspect of dorsal foot.

A 65-year-old female with past medical history of poorly controlled HIV with last known CD4 count less than 200 presents with multiple tender red spots on the tongue, arms, chest, and lips. She reports she recently rescued two cats. She denies any drug or alcohol use. Examination reveals axillary lymphadenopathy and multiple friable, dome-shaped papules and nodules on the tongue, mucosal lip, arms, and chest.

A 65-year-old female farmer with a past medical history of multiple non-melanoma skin cancers presents with a 4 week history of a dry, painful lower lip. She has tried vaseline but her lips always feel dry and sometimes are painful. She denies licking her lips frequently or any other topicals. Examination reveals atrophy of the lower vermillion border with hypopigmentation, thin scaling and scattered erythema and thin erosions with crust on the lower mucosal lip.

A 14-year-old female with no pertinent past medical history presents with a painless growing black spot on her left hand and arm. States she thinks it may have occured after working with farm animals including pigs, sheep, and cattle on her parents farm. Parents states it began as a yellow pus spot that slowly enlargened and popped with yellow fluid exiting. Review of symptoms remarkable for new shortness of breath and otherwise negative. Examination revealed an edematous pink-brown violaceous plaques with central necrotic escharsand surrounding erythema on the left hand and arm. Punch biopsy is performed and demonstrates gram positive spore-forming rods.

A 6-year-old male presents to clinic with a 2-month history of worsening itchy rash on the arms and legs that the patient constantly scratches at throughout the day. Mother reports a history of eczema and asthma. Parents deny any recent new exposures to topical products, changes in detergent. They have tried over-the-counter hydrocortisone without improvement. Examination reveals poorly demarcated lichenified plaques along the antecubital fossas and popliteal fossas bilaterally with overlying excoriations.

A 45-year-old male with no significant past medical history presents to dermatology clinic for evaluation of a rash developing on the chest, arms, back and thickened skin on the palms and soles ongoing for the past 3 months. He denies any recent travel or starting any new topical products. He denies any similar rash developing in the past. He has tried to take over the counter anti-histamines and hydrocortisone without any improvement. Review of systems is negative for joint pain or any other systemic symptoms. Examination reveals multiple bright pink-orange follicular papules coalescing into orange-red plaques with minimal scale on the chest, back, upper and lower extremities with few interspersed uninvolved areas. On the palms and soles are thickened hyperkeratotic red-orange plaques.

A 65-year-old female presents to dermatology clinic for evaluation of multiple spots on the face present since adolescence but increasing in number. Her past medical history is remarkable for multiple pulmonary cysts, spontaneous pneumothorax and renal cell carcinoma. She reports a positive family history of multiple renal cysts and recurrent pneumothorax. Physical examination reveals multiple light hypopigmented to skin colored dome shaped papules on the face and pedunculated hyperpigmented papules on the neck and axilla.

A 8-year-old female with no significant past medical history presents to the emergency room with fever, headache, malaise and rhinorrhea ongoing for past two days with recent known tick exposure. Parents deny any recent medication exposures. She is admitted to the hospital and over the next few days, she develops a rash beginning on the ankles and wrists that progressively spread onto the trunk. Physical examination reveals blanching erythematous macules on ankles, wrists, and trunk with few scattered petechiae and purpura on the bilateral ankles. She is mildly febrile and labs do not demonstrate any leukocytosis.

A 14-year-old female presenting to dermatology clinic with rosy cheeks and a history of easy sunburns and frequent respiratory infections. Physical examination demonstrates a prominent nose and ears, telangiectatic erythema in a malar distribution, and faint hypopigmentation on the cheeks.  Genetic testing is performed and reveals a BLM/RECQL3 mutation.

A 50-year-old male with no pertinent medical history presents with a two year history of dark spots on the face. He noticed the dark spots when applying make up one day. He denies any pruritus, pain, trauma or use of any new topical skin products. The dark spots have increased in number and may have slightly grown in size. He has not tried any treatments. Physical examination reveals brown irregular patchy poorly demarcated macules coalescing into patches on the bilateral zygomatic cheeks with some extension on lateral cheeks.

A 17-year-old female presents with a several year history of a spot on the neck that developed acute onset pain for the past 3 days and warmth. On examination along the left lateral neck is a tender, soft skin colored nodule. Biopsy is performed and reveals stratified squamous epithelium with surrounding lymphoid tissue.

A 56-year-old male presents with an intensely itchy patch on his right upper back for the past three years with intermittent sensations of numbness and tingling. He denies any trauma to the area. He only applies topical over the counter hydrocortisone without any relief. He denies any history of eczema and only takes multivitamins on a daily basis. Examination of the right scapula reveals a poorly defined hyperpigmented ruddy brown ovoid patch without significant lichenification.

A 6-month-old female presents to dermatology clinic with a red spot on the left forearm that was noticed a few weeks after birth. The parents note that it has become larger over the past few weeks and deny any spontaneous bleeding. The infant does not seem to be bothered by the lesion. Physical examination reveals a bright red ovoid thin plaque with telangiectasias on dermoscopy.

A 70-year-old male with past medical history of end stage renal disease on hemodialysis, coronary artery disease presents to dermatology clinic complaining of a painful rash on the right leg present for several weeks and enlargening. He admits he often misses hemodialysis sessions. Examination of the right lower leg demonstrates a retiform violaceous plaque with large black eschar. A punch biopsy reveals calcification of small and medium sized vessels with thrombosis.

A 34-year-old female presents with history of itching all over the body ongoing for the past year. She does not take any medications other than multivitamins. She denies any history of skin conditions. She has tried fexofenadine in the past which helped, but over the counter hydrocortisone only provides minimal relief. Pruritus is worse around areas of tight clothing contacting her skin that occurs within a few minutes. Skin examination reveals linear urticaria on the upper back that develop after two minutes in areas of gentle scratching with a cotton tip applicator.

A 60-year-old male presents with an intermittently tender spot on the left ear present for six months. He denies any trauma to the area but notes he often lays on the left side when sleeping at night. He denies any history of skin cancer. Examination reveals a crusted light pink papule along the left superior helix along the cartilaginous component. A biopsy is performed and reveals an ulcer with underlying dermal fibrosis with adjacent granulation tissue.

A 68-year-old male presents to dermatology for a slowly enlargening lesion on the left upper back. He denies any personal or family history of skin cancer. The lesion has been present for several years and slowly enlargening. Sometimes it gets irritated and itchy against his belt. He denies any pain or spontaneous bleeding. On examination of the left upper back is a flat topped stuck on appearing thin brown hyperkeratotic papule with milial-like cysts on dermoscopy.

A 7-year-old male presents for evaluation of facial rash that began three days ago. The patient's father reports four days before the rash began, the patient had some fevers and thigh muscle aches. Father notes many other children at the school have had a similar rash. On examination, on the bilateral cheeks are bright pink red lacy reticulated erythematous patches with sparing of the perioral and mesolabial fold with similar faint patches on the bilateral upper arms.
